On November 23, 2018, the mystery fantasy film "Fantastic Tales", which he wrote and directed, was released. On August 18, 2023, the film "Assassination Storm", for which he participated as a screenwriter, was released. On July 2, 2025, the web series "Half-Truth", for which he served as screenwriter, began airing. Evaluation

Zhou Haohui's works originated online, yet they eschew the common gimmicks of bloodiness, violence, and supernatural mystification often used in online suspense and detective novels, and do not rely on bizarre or outrageous elements as the focus to attract attention. In the chaotic online hodgepodge where click rates are paramount, compared to some impetuous, profit-driven online writers, Zhou Haohui possesses distinct personal characteristics. He courageously attempts to ensure that the popular literature prevalent on the contemporary internet is no longer confined to mere entertainment, but instead chooses to have it address social issues and demonstrate its social value. His works contain both the entertainment value sought by the masses for leisure reading and in-depth contemplation of the broader society and ordinary individuals, showing attention to and advocacy for social order and individual life. Using accessible, popular literary forms, he interprets human nature and contemporary society, endowing his works with entertainment value while also imbuing them with realism and a sense of responsibility (Han Yinan, Jilin University).

Controversies

In 2007, the novel The Girl in the Dark, written by Zhou Haohui, was allegedly plagiarized by Zhang Jiangnan's film script for Different Tomb. Not only were multiple plot points similar, but the names of the four main characters were exactly the same. Screenwriter Zhang Jiangnan claimed it was merely a coincidence. Zhou Haohui expressed his anger over the matter in two blog posts.

27

On January 19, 2016, the copyright infringement lawsuit filed by Zhou Haohui against the TV series Beauty Maker commenced at the Yangzhou Intermediate People's Court. The plaintiff, Zhou Haohui, alleged that episodes 29 and 30 of the TV series Beauty Maker copied and adapted from his novel Evil Hypnotist. He requested the defendants to cease the infringement, issue a public apology, eliminate the negative impact, and pay compensation of 831,480 yuan. The trial reconvened on March 17. During the court proceedings, both parties engaged in heated debates, each holding a different stance on whether the two works constituted "substantial similarity." As the parties failed to reach a settlement, the collegiate bench announced it would deliberate and issue a verdict at a later date.

In July 2009, his suspense novel "Detective Luo Fei Series Part 1: Death Notice" was published, and he won the Bronze Award at the 1st Online Literature Biennial Award for this novel; in the same year, he wrote the short story "Under the Bed", which was selected for the "2010 China Suspense Fiction Selection"; subsequently, his novel "Life and Death Emerald Lake" was selected for the "2009 China Suspense Literature Selection"; in September, he published the novel "Ominous Painting"; in addition, he also published the novel "Ghost Watching Slope".

2

3

Evaluation

Zhou Haohui's works originated online, yet they eschew the common gimmicks of bloodiness, violence, and supernatural mystification often used in online suspense and detective novels, and do not rely on bizarre or outrageous elements as the focus to attract attention. In the chaotic online hodgepodge where click rates are paramount, compared to some impetuous, profit-driven online writers, Zhou Haohui possesses distinct personal characteristics. He courageously attempts to ensure that the popular literature prevalent on the contemporary internet is no longer confined to mere entertainment, but instead chooses to have it address social issues and demonstrate its social value. His works contain both the entertainment value sought by the masses for leisure reading and in-depth contemplation of the broader society and ordinary individuals, showing attention to and advocacy for social order and individual life. Using accessible, popular literary forms, he interprets human nature and contemporary society, endowing his works with entertainment value while also imbuing them with realism and a sense of responsibility (Han Yinan, Jilin University).

7

Controversies

In 2007, the novel The Girl in the Dark, written by Zhou Haohui, was allegedly plagiarized by Zhang Jiangnan's film script for Different Tomb. Not only were multiple plot points similar, but the names of the four main characters were exactly the same. Screenwriter Zhang Jiangnan claimed it was merely a coincidence. Zhou Haohui expressed his anger over the matter in two blog posts.

27

On January 19, 2016, the copyright infringement lawsuit filed by Zhou Haohui against the TV series Beauty Maker commenced at the Yangzhou Intermediate People's Court. The plaintiff, Zhou Haohui, alleged that episodes 29 and 30 of the TV series Beauty Maker copied and adapted from his novel Evil Hypnotist. He requested the defendants to cease the infringement, issue a public apology, eliminate the negative impact, and pay compensation of 831,480 yuan. The trial reconvened on March 17. During the court proceedings, both parties engaged in heated debates, each holding a different stance on whether the two works constituted "substantial similarity." As the parties failed to reach a settlement, the collegiate bench announced it would deliberate and issue a verdict at a later date.

# Louis Cha, Who Wrote Beloved Chinese Martial Arts Novels As Jin Yong, Dies

 By Bill Chappell 

 Published October 31, 2018 at 5:58 PM EDT

Here, a customer reads a book at a memorial section at a bookstore in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province.](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/167c087/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2636x1977+0+0/resize/880x660!/quality/90/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fnpr-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2Flegacy%2Fimages%2Fnews%2Fnpr%2F2018%2F10%2F662571187_390507021.jpg)

Novelist Jin Yong — the pen name for writer and journalist Louis Cha — has died, triggering tributes and mourning from his fans. Here, a customer reads a book at a memorial section at a bookstore in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province.

Millions of people are mourning Jin Yong — the pen name for novelist Louis Cha — after the giant of Chinese pop culture and literature died on Tuesday. Cha wrote epic stories that created an underpinning for the pageantry and fantasy of martial arts films.Cha was 94. He died in Hong Kong, where he moved from mainland China in the 1940s to work as an author and journalist. In addition to his novels in the _wuxia_ adventure genre, Cha co-founded the newspaper _Ming Pao_, which he led for decades. His work has been translated into numerous film, TV series, and stage productions.Cha had suffered from liver cancer and dementia in his last years, the [South China Morning Post reports](https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/politics/article/2170981/hong-kong-wuxia-legend-louis-cha-battled-liver-cancer-and). Writing as Jin Yong, Cha has drawn comparisons to J.R.R. Tolkien — but that sells him short, according to [Eileen Chow](https://twitter.com/chowleen), co-director of Duke University's Story Lab project. To fully encapsulate his impact, she says, one should think of an author who combines Tolkien with George R.R. Martin, J.K. Rowling and Neil Gaiman.Spinning stories about fantastical adventures in ancient China, Cha combined action sequences with romance and emotional entanglements, giving ballast to the high-flying acrobatics of swordplay and combat. In the world of _Jianghu_(literal translation: "rivers and lakes") — the liminal sphere in which skilled knights and lethal princesses seek love and justice — Cha told complex stories that sometimes mirrored the complicated lives of Chinese who saw their society transform under Chairman Mao. Earlier this year, he acknowledged using political allegories to describe events of the Cultural Revolution, in [an interview with The New Yorker](https://www.newyorker.com/books/page-turner/the-gripping-stories-and-political-allegories-of-chinas-best-selling-author).In the process, Cha also gave readers a touchstone of the country's cultural history, creating "a China of the mind," Chow said. She added, "it would be hard to argue that there has been a more widely-read and more influential writer in Chinese in the modern era."Comparing Cha to Shakespeare, former _Morning Post_ writer Oliver Chou[told the newspaper](https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/society/article/2170910/hong-kongs-most-famous-martial-arts-writer-louis-cha-dies), "No other Chinese authors would appeal so much to Chinese readers, regardless of dialects and political views. The late paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping, was said to have sent secret agents to get him a set of Cha's novels in Hong Kong in the early 1980s."In one famous example of the hidden complexity found in Cha's work, the first letters from the titles of his 14 martial arts novels create an acrostic couplet. According to a [translation by Chow](https://twitter.com/chowleen/status/1057339338495803392), it reads: _Whirling snow blankets the sky, I hunt white deer   
Laughing as I write legends of chivalry and romance._ Novels penned by Jin Yong began appearing in serial form in 1955, with _The Book and the Sword._ In the years that followed, the stories often appeared in Cha's own newspaper."He is best-known for his martial arts fiction series _The Condor Trilogy_," NPR's Rob Schmitz reports from Shanghai, adding that Cha's books have sold more than 300 million copies worldwide. _The Condor Trilogy_ also features one of Cha's most memorable characters: Huang Rong, who runs away from her family, poses as a beggar boy, learns the intricacies of deadly kung fu, and uses her intellect and guile to help her lover, Guo Jing, defeat his enemies. Her skills range from succulent cooking to mastery of the secret Dog Beating Staff fighting style.The role has been played by many actresses — so many that [Asia One held an online poll in 2017](http://www.asiaone.com/showbiz/which-actress-was-best-huang-rong-condor-heroes) to ask who had done it best.Besides his writing, Cha was also known for his involvement in politics. He was part of the Hong Kong committee that monitored the territory's transfer of sovereignty to China in 1997. Years earlier, he resigned from a separate committee to protest the deadly 1989 crackdown in Beijing's Tiananmen Square."He was an advocate of democracy and freedom," Schmitz says. "One of his most famous lines is: 'Life is like a fight. Then, you leave quietly.' "To get a sense of the far reach of Cha's influence, consider that his ardent fans include Jack Ma, the billionaire founder of retail giant Alibaba. As news of the author's death spread, Ma — a former English teacher — posted photos of himself and Cha, along with a lengthy message [on the social media site Weibo](https://www.weibo.com/2145291155/H0vkig5A4?type=comment#_rnd1541000385621). In his post, Ma praised Cha for teaching lessons of bravery, dedication and integrity.Without Cha, Ma said, there would be no Alibaba. He even borrowed his own nickname, Feng Qingyang, from a master swordsman in the 1967 novel _The Smiling, Proud Wanderer_. He encouraged Alibaba employees to choose their own characters from his works. And as [Ming Pao reports](https://www.mpfinance.com/fin/instantf2.php?node=1540972686758&issue=20181031), Ma named his own office and other parts of Alibaba's headquarters after places in Cha's stories. After _The Deer And The Cauldron_ was published (again, in serial form) in 1972, Cha stopped writing martial arts novels. And in the last decades of his life, the author faced one nagging problem: the constant demand from his legion of fans that he write more books for them to read."I'm getting old, and my imagination is not the same as it was in my younger days," Cha [told The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/1989/01/03/books/chinese-demand-more-by-a-literary-legend.html) in 1989. The world may not have known the richness of Cha's imagination, had he not been pressed into service as a serial novelist. As the _Times_ noted in that profile, Cha was a young copy editor when he was asked to come on as a temp, simply because his newspaper's fiction writer had resigned. Copyright 2018 NPR. # Louis Cha, Who Wrote Beloved Chinese Martial Arts Novels As Jin Yong, Dies

 By Bill Chappell 

 Published October 31, 2018 at 5:58 PM EDT 

*   [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?app_id=555249582300604&display=popup&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ideastream.org%2F2018-10-31%2Flouis-cha-who-wrote-beloved-chinese-martial-arts-novels-as-jin-yong-dies)

![Image 5: Novelist Jin Yong — the pen name for writer and journalist Louis Cha — has died, triggering tributes and mourning from his fans. Here, a customer reads a book at a memorial section at a bookstore in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province.](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/167c087/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2636x1977+0+0/resize/880x660!/quality/90/?url=http%3A%2F%2Fnpr-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2Flegacy%2Fimages%2Fnews%2Fnpr%2F2018%2F10%2F662571187_390507021.jpg)

Novelist Jin Yong — the pen name for writer and journalist Louis Cha — has died, triggering tributes and mourning from his fans. Here, a customer reads a book at a memorial section at a bookstore in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province.

Millions of people are mourning Jin Yong — the pen name for novelist Louis Cha — after the giant of Chinese pop culture and literature died on Tuesday. Cha wrote epic stories that created an underpinning for the pageantry and fantasy of martial arts films.Cha was 94. He died in Hong Kong, where he moved from mainland China in the 1940s to work as an author and journalist. In addition to his novels in the _wuxia_ adventure genre, Cha co-founded the newspaper _Ming Pao_, which he led for decades. His work has been translated into numerous film, TV series, and stage productions.Cha had suffered from liver cancer and dementia in his last years, the [South China Morning Post reports](https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/politics/article/2170981/hong-kong-wuxia-legend-louis-cha-battled-liver-cancer-and). Writing as Jin Yong, Cha has drawn comparisons to J.R.R. Tolkien — but that sells him short, according to [Eileen Chow](https://twitter.com/chowleen), co-director of Duke University's Story Lab project. To fully encapsulate his impact, she says, one should think of an author who combines Tolkien with George R.R. Martin, J.K. Rowling and Neil Gaiman.Spinning stories about fantastical adventures in ancient China, Cha combined action sequences with romance and emotional entanglements, giving ballast to the high-flying acrobatics of swordplay and combat. In the world of _Jianghu_(literal translation: "rivers and lakes") — the liminal sphere in which skilled knights and lethal princesses seek love and justice — Cha told complex stories that sometimes mirrored the complicated lives of Chinese who saw their society transform under Chairman Mao. Earlier this year, he acknowledged using political allegories to describe events of the Cultural Revolution, in [an interview with The New Yorker](https://www.newyorker.com/books/page-turner/the-gripping-stories-and-political-allegories-of-chinas-best-selling-author).In the process, Cha also gave readers a touchstone of the country's cultural history, creating "a China of the mind," Chow said. She added, "it would be hard to argue that there has been a more widely-read and more influential writer in Chinese in the modern era."Comparing Cha to Shakespeare, former _Morning Post_ writer Oliver Chou[told the newspaper](https://www.scmp.com/news/hong-kong/society/article/2170910/hong-kongs-most-famous-martial-arts-writer-louis-cha-dies), "No other Chinese authors would appeal so much to Chinese readers, regardless of dialects and political views. The late paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping, was said to have sent secret agents to get him a set of Cha's novels in Hong Kong in the early 1980s."In one famous example of the hidden complexity found in Cha's work, the first letters from the titles of his 14 martial arts novels create an acrostic couplet. According to a [translation by Chow](https://twitter.com/chowleen/status/1057339338495803392), it reads: _Whirling snow blankets the sky, I hunt white deer   
Laughing as I write legends of chivalry and romance._ Novels penned by Jin Yong began appearing in serial form in 1955, with _The Book and the Sword._ In the years that followed, the stories often appeared in Cha's own newspaper."He is best-known for his martial arts fiction series _The Condor Trilogy_," NPR's Rob Schmitz reports from Shanghai, adding that Cha's books have sold more than 300 million copies worldwide. _The Condor Trilogy_ also features one of Cha's most memorable characters: Huang Rong, who runs away from her family, poses as a beggar boy, learns the intricacies of deadly kung fu, and uses her intellect and guile to help her lover, Guo Jing, defeat his enemies. Her skills range from succulent cooking to mastery of the secret Dog Beating Staff fighting style.The role has been played by many actresses — so many that [Asia One held an online poll in 2017](http://www.asiaone.com/showbiz/which-actress-was-best-huang-rong-condor-heroes) to ask who had done it best.Besides his writing, Cha was also known for his involvement in politics. He was part of the Hong Kong committee that monitored the territory's transfer of sovereignty to China in 1997. Years earlier, he resigned from a separate committee to protest the deadly 1989 crackdown in Beijing's Tiananmen Square."He was an advocate of democracy and freedom," Schmitz says. "One of his most famous lines is: 'Life is like a fight. Then, you leave quietly.' "To get a sense of the far reach of Cha's influence, consider that his ardent fans include Jack Ma, the billionaire founder of retail giant Alibaba. As news of the author's death spread, Ma — a former English teacher — posted photos of himself and Cha, along with a lengthy message [on the social media site Weibo](https://www.weibo.com/2145291155/H0vkig5A4?type=comment#_rnd1541000385621). In his post, Ma praised Cha for teaching lessons of bravery, dedication and integrity.Without Cha, Ma said, there would be no Alibaba. He even borrowed his own nickname, Feng Qingyang, from a master swordsman in the 1967 novel _The Smiling, Proud Wanderer_. He encouraged Alibaba employees to choose their own characters from his works. And as [Ming Pao reports](https://www.mpfinance.com/fin/instantf2.php?node=1540972686758&issue=20181031), Ma named his own office and other parts of Alibaba's headquarters after places in Cha's stories. After _The Deer And The Cauldron_ was published (again, in serial form) in 1972, Cha stopped writing martial arts novels. And in the last decades of his life, the author faced one nagging problem: the constant demand from his legion of fans that he write more books for them to read."I'm getting old, and my imagination is not the same as it was in my younger days," Cha [told The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/1989/01/03/books/chinese-demand-more-by-a-literary-legend.html) in 1989. The world may not have known the richness of Cha's imagination, had he not been pressed into service as a serial novelist. As the _Times_ noted in that profile, Cha was a young copy editor when he was asked to come on as a temp, simply because his newspaper's fiction writer had resigned. Copyright 2018 NPR. ## Abstract

Recent studies have convincingly mapped the literary beginnings of the modern Chinese novel since the 1890s. However, the pivotal role of the Shenbaoguan publishing house and its British owner and manager Ernest Major during the previous two decades in creating the material, market, and cultural conditions for this rise of the modern novel has been neglected, mostly because the label “cultural imperialism” is widely attached to this foreign-owned company. This essay maps the dominant role of Shenbaoguan in publishing Chinese-language novels between 1872 and 1890 (after first opting for translations of Western novels) and the strategies it devised to elevate the cultural standing of the novel from its previous low ranking as a literary genre. These strategies included a prestigious, imperial publishing format with high-quality modern printing technology; careful manuscript selection in often close interaction with an evolving Shenbaoguan community; fixed pricing; a national distribution network, and a rich body of paratexts such as titles written by famous calligraphers, prefaces by prominent men-of-letters, tables of contents, commentaries, lists of dramatis personae, and, last but not least, an aesthetic appreciation in Shenbao announcements and special catalogs that reinforced the novel’s new standing.

4.   The company integrated Western and Chinese literary practices, redefining the novel's role in a modern context.
5.   Women readers were targeted in novel selections, reflecting changing social attitudes towards female literacy and authorship.

First, the author shows that the ancient “study of wen” or wenxue—the word later used to translate “literature” in modern Chinese—has been seen by a Jesuit in the seventeenth century as an equivalent of rhetoric, and that this premodern discipline, at least in that period, resembled more the “study of wen” than the modern, post-eighteenth century “literature”: the object of rhetoric, like the object of the “study of wen,” was an “ornamented” form of writing that could be found in both “literary” and “non-literary” genres, and it was associated to both courtly and administrative uses of writing. Second, the author explains in more detail the ornamental and trans-generic features of the imperial wen. By following a number of texts from medieval times to the nineteenth century, he argues that the association between wen, literati sociability, and court and administrative practices, recurrently shaped discussions on text composition in imperial history until the late Qing (1644-1912). Third, and last, he deals with two strategies of reconceptualization of writing at the time when court society and imperial institutions were losing their central position as sources of authority for late Qing literati. The author argues that modern “literature” was just one strategy among others of reconciling the old wen with the demands of the modern concept of “nation”—a strategy that, in some respects, would be unable to expunge wen of the hierarchical inspiration it inherited from the ancient social order. By exposing different ways of conceptualizing aesthetic experience with writing, and by claiming that “literature” was only one conceptual strategy among others, this part of the essay contributes to an understanding of “literature” not as the necessary result of “modernization” or as a trans-historical institution, but as a contingency, as something that was not inevitable in modern Chinese history.

## Abstract

Recent studies have convincingly mapped the literary beginnings of the modern Chinese novel since the 1890s. However, the pivotal role of the Shenbaoguan publishing house and its British owner and manager Ernest Major during the previous two decades in creating the material, market, and cultural conditions for this rise of the modern novel has been neglected, mostly because the label “cultural imperialism” is widely attached to this foreign-owned company. This essay maps the dominant role of Shenbaoguan in publishing Chinese-language novels between 1872 and 1890 (after first opting for translations of Western novels) and the strategies it devised to elevate the cultural standing of the novel from its previous low ranking as a literary genre. These strategies included a prestigious, imperial publishing format with high-quality modern printing technology; careful manuscript selection in often close interaction with an evolving Shenbaoguan community; fixed pricing; a national distribution network, and a rich body of paratexts such as titles written by famous calligraphers, prefaces by prominent men-of-letters, tables of contents, commentaries, lists of dramatis personae, and, last but not least, an aesthetic appreciation in Shenbao announcements and special catalogs that reinforced the novel’s new standing.

How could modern “literature” emerge in China? And what was its relation to the imperial ways of conceptualizing writing? This essay argues that modern “literature” was just one strategy among others of reconceptualizing the use of writing in late-nineteenth and early-twentieth century China. First, the author shows that the ancient “study of wen” or wenxue—the word later used to translate “literature” in modern Chinese—has been seen by a Jesuit in the seventeenth century as an equivalent of rhetoric, and that this premodern discipline, at least in that period, resembled more the “study of wen” than the modern, post-eighteenth century “literature”: the object of rhetoric, like the object of the “study of wen,” was an “ornamented” form of writing that could be found in both “literary” and “non-literary” genres, and it was associated to both courtly and administrative uses of writing. Second, the author explains in more detail the ornamental and trans-generic features of the imperial wen. By following a number of texts from medieval times to the nineteenth century, he argues that the association between wen, literati sociability, and court and administrative practices, recurrently shaped discussions on text composition in imperial history until the late Qing (1644-1912). Third, and last, he deals with two strategies of reconceptualization of writing at the time when court society and imperial institutions were losing their central position as sources of authority for late Qing literati. The author argues that modern “literature” was just one strategy among others of reconciling the old wen with the demands of the modern concept of “nation”—a strategy that, in some respects, would be unable to expunge wen of the hierarchical inspiration it inherited from the ancient social order. By exposing different ways of conceptualizing aesthetic experience with writing, and by claiming that “literature” was only one conceptual strategy among others, this part of the essay contributes to an understanding of “literature” not as the necessary result of “modernization” or as a trans-historical institution, but as a contingency, as something that was not inevitable in modern Chinese history.

# Top Chinese language novelist dies in apparent suicide

4 December 2024

Share

Save

[Add as preferred on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=bbc.com)

Fan Wang BBC News

![Image 1: Getty Images Chiung Yao attends a press conference on July 10, 2007 in Taipei.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/1936/live/72bf77b0-b216-11ef-a7e9-e72ab6369e72.jpg.webp)Getty Images

Chiung Yao, arguably the world's most popular Chinese language romance novelist, has died in an apparent suicide.

The 86-year-old's body was found in her home in New Taipei City on Wednesday, local media report. Emergency services said she took her own life, according to Taiwan's Central News Agency.

Chiung Yao started writing at 18 and published more than 60 novels, many of which were adapted into movies and TV series and remained popular for decades.

She was also a successful screenwriter and producer. One of her most famous works was the TV drama My Fair Princess, which launched the careers of big name stars.

She was born Chen Che in Sichuan, China in 1938. Chiung Yao is her pen name.

A post on her Facebook account on Wednesday read: "Goodbye, my loved ones. I feel lucky that I have met and known you in this life". It was not immediately clear if the post was published before or after her body was found.

Chiung Yao asked young people "not to give up on life easily" and to confront death only when "you live until 86 or 87". She asked her followers not to be sad for her.

She has not been active in recent years. However, she made headlines in 2017 after her dispute with her stepchildren over how to care for her then ailing husband came into public view.

Chiung Yao spent part of her childhood in mainland China as her family moved across the country during the Sino-Japanese War.

The family moved to Taiwan in 1949 after the Chinese Communist Party took control of the mainland.

![Image 2: Getty Images Actress Zhao Wei (left) and Fan Bingbing attend the 8th China Film Directors' Guild Awards on April 22, 2017 in Beijing](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/news/480/cpsprodpb/3214/live/cd4e64b0-b21c-11ef-a60f-2583ac5097f7.jpg.webp)Getty Images

Chiung Yao's TV drama My Fair Princess launced the careers of Zhao Wei (left) and Fan Bingbing

Chiung Yao's debut novel Outside The Window, which was inspired by her own love story with her high school teacher, was hugely popular.

Her TV drama My Fair Princess, a Cinderella story set in the 18th century Qing Dynasty, is regarded as one of the most popular Chinese-language drama shows of all time.

It launched the careers of big names in entertainment, including Chinese superstar Fan Bingbing. Fan would go on to become one of the biggest stars in China, until she was [fined for tax fraud in 2018](https://www.bbc.com/news/business-45728459).

The show’s main actors, Ruby Lin and Zhao Wei, became household names to Chinese audiences.

Lin has remained active as an actor and producer in Taiwan. However Zhao has been silent in recent years after her billionaire friend, Alibaba founder Jack Ma, got into trouble with the authorities in Beijing.

Qiong Yao (April 20, 1938 – December 4, 2024), born Chen Zhe, was born in Chengdu, Sichuan, with ancestral roots in Hengyang, Hunan. She was a contemporary Chinese writer, screenwriter, and film and television producer.

In 1949, she moved with her parents from mainland China to Taiwan. She began her writing career during her high school years. In 1955, she published the novel Cloud Shadows under the pen name Xin Ru. In 1963, she published her first full-length novel Outside the Window, which brought her fame. In 1964, she published the novel Misty Rain and the story collection Six Dreams, among other works. In 1975, she released the novel By the Water. In 1985, she entered the film and television production industry, and the TV series Several Times the Sunset Glows Red, which she produced, achieved great success. In 1989, she published her autobiography My Story. From 1990 to 1993, TV series she produced, such as Wan Jun and The Plum Blossom Brand, were broadcast. In 1998, the TV series My Fair Princess, for which she wrote the screenplay and served as producer, aired and later won the 17th China TV Golden Eagle Award for Best Long Series. In 2001, the TV series Romance in the Rain, for which she wrote the screenplay and served as producer, was broadcast. In 2018, she compiled and published the Qiong Yao Complete Works. In 2019, she completed the novel Plum Blossom Hero Dream. On December 4, 2024, Qiong Yao passed away at her home at the age of 86.

1

Qiong Yao's creative career spanned multiple fields including novels, essays, and screenplays. Many of her works have been adapted into films and television series, becoming a shared memory for several generations of audiences. In the eyes of readers, Qiong Yao's works are characterized by smooth and elegant prose, intricate and touching stories, and a fresh and romantic atmosphere, filled with a longing for dreams and a persistence in love. Her works are closely integrated with popular culture and are widely circulated on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, Hong Kong, and Macau.

Life Experience

Early Years

On the early morning of April 20, 1938, Qiong Yao was born at the Renji Hospital on Sishengci Street in Chengdu. She lived in Chengdu until she was four years old. In 1942, she moved with her parents back to the ancestral home, "Lanzhi Hall," in Hengyang, Hunan. From the summer of 1944 to the autumn of 1945, under the influence of the War of Resistance Against Japan, she fled with her parents from Hunan to Chongqing. Subsequently, she settled with her mother at the Lu County Lu'nan Middle School in Sichuan. In 1947, she moved with her family to Shanghai and entered school for the first time (Shanghai Sixteenth District National Primary School, today's Hongkou District First Central Primary School). In 1948, she returned to Hengyang with her mother and enrolled at Hengyang Gangzhi Primary School. In the summer of 1949, she moved with her parents to Taipei City, Taiwan Province; in the autumn of the same year, she transferred into the sixth grade at Taipei Normal University Affiliated Primary School. In 1950, she graduated from Taipei Normal University Affiliated Primary School and was admitted to Taipei First Girls' High School.

2

Writing Career

Initial Phase

In 1947, while in primary school, Qiong Yao was deeply inspired by viewing the wall newspapers created by upper-grade students and subsequently became fascinated with writing. She often used the daily conversations between her parents as material, and the content she created frequently made her parents laugh heartily. Soon after, she asked her father to help submit her exercise piece "Poor Little Qing" to the Shanghai-based newspaper "Ta Kung Pao." On December 6, 1947, "Poor Little Qing" was published in the "Modern Children" column on page 9 of "Ta Kung Pao."

2

![Image 6: Qiong Yao's "Poor Little Qing"](https://gbaike-image.cdn.bcebos.com/91529822720e0cf3d7cabba66d1fe51fbe096b637c6e/91529822720e0cf3d7cabba66d1fe51fbe096b637c6e_url?x-bce-process=image/format,f_auto/resize,m_lfit,h_400,limit_1)

Qiong Yao's "Poor Little Qing"

![Image 7: December 6, 1947, Ta Kung Pao](https://gbaike-image.cdn.bcebos.com/91529822720e0cf3d7cabba76d1fe51fbe096b637c6f/91529822720e0cf3d7cabba76d1fe51fbe096b637c6f_3_4?x-bce-process=image/format,f_auto)

December 6, 1947, Ta Kung Pao

In 1954, after graduating from junior high school, she was admitted to Taipei Second Girls' High School (now Zhongshan Girls' High School). In her first year of high school, she attempted suicide by taking pills due to poor math grades. In 1955, she published the short story "Cloud Shadows" in the Taiwanese magazine "Morning Light" under the pen name Xin Ru. In 1957, after failing the college entrance exam, she again attempted suicide by taking pills. In July 1958, after failing the college entrance exam a second time, she resolved not to retake the exam and firmly pursued her dream of writing, but several novels she wrote were rejected by publishers. In 1961, she completed the short story "Lover's Valley," which was published in the magazine "Crown."

2

In 1963, drawing from her own experiences, she completed her first full-length novel, "Outside the Window," which was 200,000 characters long. One week after mailing it to the magazine "Crown," she received a letter confirming its publication. It was later published in the "Book of the Month" column of issue 113 of "Crown" magazine. In July, her novella "The Pursuit" was serialized in the supplement of Taiwan's "United Daily News," attracting attention. In September, *Outside the Window* was published as a single-volume book with an initial print run of 1,000 copies. Upon release, it sold out multiple times and was widely praised.

19

Professional Writer

In 1964, she moved to Taipei to settle down and devoted herself to writing. She published three full-length novels, "Misty Rain," "Several Times the Sunset Glows Red," and "Dodder Flower," as well as the collection of novellas and short stories "Six Dreams" and "Lucky Grass."

19

In 1965, she sold the film rights for her novel "Six Dreams" to Taiwan's Central Motion Picture Corporation. Two of the stories, "The Pursuit" and "Mute Wife," were selected for film adaptation. After the films were released, they became very popular. After watching the films in the cinema, Qiong Yao became fascinated with adapting her novels for the screen.

19

In 1966, she published the full-length novels "Purple Shell," "The Boat," and "Cold Mist Green."

3

In 1967, she and Ping Xintao established the Firebird Film Company (which dissolved in 1969). The following year, she adapted the novel "Lucky Grass" to produce the films "Full Moon Over the West Tower" and "Stranger." In 1976, she, along with Ping Xintao and others, established the Giant Star Film Company, which successfully adapted and filmed "Cloud of Romance." In 1983, weary of film production, she decisively closed down the Giant Star Company.

2

In 1985, she and Ping Xintao established the Yiren Communication Company, entering the television industry. They launched the TV series "Several Times the Sunset Glows Red," the first television drama adapted from a Qiong Yao novel, which generated considerable response. The success of "Several Times the Sunset Glows Red" not only led some television stations to adapt other works by Qiong Yao, such as "I Am a Cloud" and "By the Water," but also enabled Taiwanese TV dramas, represented by Qiong Yao's romance dramas, to enter mainland China.

8

In 1988, she visited mainland China for the first time to see relatives, traveling to Beijing, Hubei, Sichuan, Yunnan, and other places, and began compiling her complete works.

2

In January 1989, she published her mainland travelogue "Unbreakable Nostalgia." In May, she returned to Hengyang, Hunan, to pay respects to her ancestors. During this period, she established a cooperative relationship with Hunan Television, actively promoting cross-strait co-production of the TV series "Six Dreams" series, which was completed the following year with "Wan Jun," "Mute Wife," and "Three Flowers," featuring famous cultural landmarks from across the country. In October, she compiled old manuscripts and published her autobiography "My Story," recounting her life story and writing experience.

Personal Life

Family

Qiong Yao's father was Chen Zhiping, a native of Hengyang, Hunan, and a historian. His works include "Lectures on Qin and Han History," "Lectures on Three Kingdoms History," and "General History of China."

30

Qiong Yao's mother was Yuan Xingshu, the eldest daughter of Yuan Lizhen, the eldest son of Liangnan scholar Yuan Xuechang and the renowned female Chinese medicine practitioner and poet Zeng Yi. She was originally from Wujin, Jiangsu, but grew up in Beijing. Hailing from a family of scholars, she was fond of classical literature from a young age and graduated from Beiping (Beijing) Art College.

Romantic Relationships

While in high school, Qiong Yao fell in love with her Chinese literature teacher, who was 25 years her senior and a widower. Later, after failing the university entrance exam, their student-teacher relationship was exposed. Qiong Yao's mother reported their relationship to the "Police Department" and the "Ministry of Education" on the grounds of "seduction of a minor" and "student enticement." The teacher was subsequently dismissed from his school and left Taipei.

7

Qiong Yao's first husband was Ma Senqing. The two married in 1959 and later had a son named Chen Zhongwei. Their marital conflicts deepened following the publication of "*Outside the Window*." In the spring of 1964, they divorced.

2

Qiong Yao's second husband was Ping Xintao. Their relationship began with manuscript solicitations. Over the next few years, they met, got to know each other, co-founded a company, becoming business partners and gradually coming together in their personal lives as well. On May 9, 1979, more than a decade after first meeting, Qiong Yao and Ping Xintao married. Ping Xintao passed away on May 23, 2019.

28

Death

At approximately 13:22 on December 4, 2024, Qiong Yao passed away at her home in Tamsui District, New Taipei City, Taiwan Province. According to her son, Qiong Yao had instructed her secretary, Shu Ling, to check on her at home around noon. The secretary entered the residence and found Qiong Yao had taken her own life in her room. Upon seeing this, the secretary immediately notified emergency services (119). However, when rescue personnel arrived, they found Qiong Yao had no breath or pulse and was clearly deceased, so she was not taken to a hospital. Police from Tamsui arrived at the scene after receiving the report and preliminarily ruled out external interference. Subsequently, Secretary Shu Ling posted Qiong Yao's suicide note and a recitation video titled "When Snowflakes Fall" on behalf of Qiong Yao on Qiong Yao's Facebook fan page. The suicide note mentioned that Qiong Yao had "fluttered away" and hoped the public would not grieve for her. On the same day, following a legal examination by the prosecutor, preliminary results were announced, determining no suspicion of homicide. According to Taiwanese media reports, Qiong Yao died from asphyxiation due to carbon monoxide poisoning.

Creative Characteristics

Works Mirroring Personal Experience

Starting with Outside the Window in 1963, the romance novels created by Qiong Yao have influenced several generations. The theme of love runs through Qiong Yao's works, but the specific changes in endings and styles highly correspond with her own life experiences. In her early period, Qiong Yao favored tragedies. Her first full-length novel, Outside the Window, was a tragedy. At that time, Qiong Yao had just experienced a fruitless teacher-student romance, which cast a gloomy shadow over her understanding of love. The teacher-student romance depicted in the book bore traces of her own life. Subsequently, Qiong Yao married a husband who also loved writing, but they later separated due to writing, leading to the sentimental and oppressive characteristics evident in her works from this period. After Outside the Window, she successively published novels such as Misty Rain, Six Dreams, Lucky Grass, Several Times the Sunset Glows Red, Dodder Flower, and Sound of the Tide. Most of these works ended in tragedy. In her autobiography My Story, Qiong Yao detailed her decade-long extramarital affair with Ping Xintao. This painful and entangled extramarital relationship became material for her writing, as reflected in works like Purple Shell, I Am a Cloud, and Wave.

In the mid-1970s, during Qiong Yao's middle writing period, she and Ping Xintao, who had been in love for over a decade, finally came together, which had a tremendous impact on her creation. Beginning with Heart Has a Thousand Knots in 1973, Qiong Yao's writing style shifted towards a brighter and more optimistic tone. Although characters still endured many hardships, tragedies were minimized as much as possible, resulting in happy endings. After the 1990s, Princess Pearl maximized the comedic effect. In Qiong Yao's later works, through different characters and love stories, she repeatedly conveyed one viewpoint—"love possesses the power to overcome everything."

32

Meeting the Needs of the Era

Discussing the reasons for the "Qiong Yao fever," some scholars believe that the mid-to-late 1980s coincided with an era of ideological liberation, where sensory entertainment and recreational literature gradually prevailed. The emergence of Qiong Yao's works met the needs of the times. In the 1990s and early 21st century, cultural works diversified, causing Qiong Yao to be temporarily overshadowed. After entering the 21st century, Qiong Yao once again resonated with the modern "light aesthetic era," where literature and film are merely prepared for sensory entertainment and emotional release. Qiong Yao became the spokesperson for the light aesthetic era once more, her trajectory aligning with the era's path from beginning to end. Zhang Yiwu, a professor in the Chinese Department of Peking University, analyzed that in the 1960s, Taiwan was undergoing economic transformation, and people's concepts were changing dramatically, a situation very similar to the changes occurring in mainland China in the 1980s. Qiong Yao's novels had a profound influence on Chinese society at that time. Qiong Yao's works fully express a nostalgia for traditional values as well as an attitude of adapting to the changes of the new era.

32

Describing Emotion Itself

The love in Qiong Yao's works is essentially isolated, stripped of all social attributes. The most classic example is her earlier work Wan Jun. Qiong Yao's romance novels evolved from the Mandarin Duck and Butterfly School of the 1920s and 1930s. The difference is that the love presented in Mandarin Duck and Butterfly School novels was mostly sorrowful, closely related to the overall societal oppression and heaviness. Qiong Yao inherited the "emotion" from the Mandarin Duck and Butterfly School but removed the "sorrow," resulting in an overflowing sentiment. This sentiment does not point to anything; emotion points to emotion itself. In her works, love is both the form and the content. Precisely because Qiong Yao's love stories shed much of their mundane worldly aspects, they have been welcomed by several generations of young people. Descriptions of love triangles and extramarital affairs in Qiong Yao's works serve the need for dramatic construction in the novels; they are matters of novelistic technique.

32

Influence

Unique Literary Model

The love depicted by Qiong Yao is not the love of mortal flesh, but rather a transcendent, otherworldly love akin to that portrayed by Dante in Divina Commedia. The theme of love in Qiong Yao's novels is not grounded in real life but rooted in an ideal kingdom, a point for which she is often criticized. Qiong Yao does not reproduce life as it is, but rather portrays life as it should be. She depicts an ideal world, not stories from real life.

Among the numerous romance writers in Taiwan, Qiong Yao is quite distinctive. Over her decades-long career in writing romance novels, Qiong Yao developed a unique style in terms of characters, themes, structure, language, and other aspects. Her particular life experiences and aesthetic pursuits led her early novels to favor tragedy, while her later works distinctly reject and deconstruct it. Qiong Yao's novels exhibit a tendency toward formulaic patterns in plot structure, characters, themes, and language, forming the distinctive "Qiong Yao model." In the history of modern and contemporary Chinese romance literature, Qiong Yao is a writer who connects the past and the future. On one hand, she inherits the literary traditions of predecessors like Zhang Henshui, while on the other hand, her creative model has influenced contemporary and later writers such as San Mao and Yi Shu.

36

Perfecting the Film System

The significance of Qiong Yao's literary films lies not only in opening up a distinctive tradition of genre films for the development of Taiwanese cinema but also in inheriting the commercial film tradition with strong popular cultural overtones that has been evolving since the birth of Chinese cinema. The emergence, development, and widespread influence of Qiong Yao's films in Chinese communities are, in fact, powerful proof of the shared cultural roots and continuous development across the strait. Qiong Yao's films created a prosperous landscape for Taiwanese cinema, making outstanding contributions to the perfection of its commercial system. This also represents a form of genre shaping during the early stages of Taiwanese film development.

Qiong Yao's films interweave the unique nostalgic consciousness, Chinese complex, and modern concepts of Taiwanese people, presenting a true picture of Taiwanese society. Consequently, Qiong Yao's films possess unique cultural value. This cultural value, combined with the commercial success they achieved at the box office in the 1960s and 1970s, inevitably secures Qiong Yao's films an important place in the history of Taiwanese cinema.

37

Overseas Export of Works

In the 1990s, Princess Pearl caused a sensation in Southeast Asia, Europe, and America, with Vietnam producing a local remake. Foreigners left comments on "C-drama" (Chinese TV drama) forums saying, "When Yi Ping fainted on the stairs, I burst into tears." Foreigners who enjoy C-dramas call themselves Chinenglish Bilingual (Cfan). They follow Chinese TV dramas and variety shows, form interest groups, and critique acting skills. The influence of Chinese TV dramas began to spread overseas, forming an increasingly large overseas fan base for these shows. The "Chinese Wave" is becoming a new force in cultural export.

38

Critical Assessment

In Qiong Yao's works, the characters are not troubled by concerns over food and clothing, and instead are wholeheartedly entangled in matters of emotion. (Comment by writer Wang Anyi)

21

Poetic charm and picturesque beauty are distinguishing features of Qiong Yao's novels. The extensive use of classical poetry, lyrics, and prose endows the originally popular romance fiction with an extraordinary, ethereal elegance. (Comment by Yangcheng Evening News)

22

Although most of the female characters portrayed by Qiong Yao are distinct and possess a sense of independence, some of her views on gender roles remain quite traditional: a woman does not have to be beautiful but must be youthful; a woman who cannot win a man's affection is not a good woman. (Comment by scholar Lin Fangmei)

22

Although, viewed as a whole, the intellectual merit and standard of Qiong Yao's works are uneven, a considerable number of her works possess positive and profound ideological depth. Works such as Misty Rain, Several Times the Sunset Glows Red, and A Red Bean all have commendable aspects in their thematic concerns. For example, Misty Rain integrates marriage and romance into a historical context. Through the rise and fall of the family of Lu Zhenhua, who once dominated much of China, it reflects, from one perspective, decades of turmoil and transformation in Chinese history, and presents a relatively objective depiction of the inevitable trajectory of historical progress. (Comment from A General History of Chinese Literature)

23

Qiong Yao provided a new literary framework for a weak generation, ossifying their thinking and leading them down the path of becoming obedient subjects. (Comment by writer Li Ao)

22

Many of Qiong Yao's novels have been adapted into film and television works, enjoying immense popularity across the Chinese-speaking world. (Comment by Xinhua Net)

73

Several of Qiong Yao's novelistic works have been adapted into widely acclaimed films or television series, including Princess Pearl and A Dream Behind the Curtain, and enjoy great fame in the Chinese-speaking world. (Comment by China Youth Daily)

74

Posthumous Commemoration

On December 4, 2024, the passing of writer Qiong Yao triggered collective mourning from numerous actors who had portrayed roles in her dramas, screenwriters, and celebrities who had collaborated with her. Actors such as Angel, Ma Yili, Tamia Liu, Li Sheng, Brigitte Lin, Qin Lan, Chen Derong, and Ming Jin took to social media, recalling their encounters and collaborative experiences with Qiong Yao, expressing their gratitude and remembrance for her. Simultaneously, Qiong Yao's apprentice, screenwriter Shen Zhining, also shared old photos in tribute.

45

On December 6, 2024, the China Writers Association sent a condolence telegram to the family of Ms. Qiong Yao, expressing grief over her passing and offering condolences to her relatives.

80

On December 7, 2024, at Qiong Yao's ancestral home, Lanzhi Hall, in Hengyang, Hunan, villagers held a memorial activity, braving the rain to bid farewell to Qiong Yao.

79

On December 11, 2024, at a press conference of the Taiwan Affairs Office, spokesperson Zhu Fenglian stated that Ms. Qiong Yao was a highly influential Taiwanese writer who harbored deep affection for the Chinese mainland and played a positive role in promoting cross-strait exchanges and film and television cooperation. We express profound condolences for the passing of Ms. Qiong Yao and extend sincere sympathies to her family.

Controversies

Copyright Dispute

On April 20, 2014, Qiong Yao expressed dissatisfaction that Yu Zheng's new drama "Coming Home: The Lost Daughter" plagiarized her earlier work "Plum Blossom Brand." She sent an open letter to the State Administration of Press, Publication, Radio, Film and Television, condemning Yu Zheng's infringement. In May, Qiong Yao filed a lawsuit against Yu Zheng, the screenwriter of "Palace: The Lock Heart Jade," and the production company for infringing the copyright of "Plum Blossom Brand." The case was accepted by the Beijing Third Intermediate People's Court. On December 18, 2015, the final judgment in Qiong Yao's copyright protection case for "Plum Blossom Brand" was delivered. The ruling determined that "Palace: The Lock Heart Jade" infringed upon the adaptation and filming rights of "Plum Blossom Brand." The defendants were ordered to cease the infringement, Yu Zheng was required to apologize to Qiong Yao, and the defendants were to compensate the plaintiff 5 million yuan. In May 2018, because Yu Zheng, who was found liable for infringement, had delayed apologizing to Qiong Yao, the Third Intermediate Court, in accordance with the judgment, published the case details in the "Legal Daily" as an announcement. On May 23, the full cost of this announcement, 336,000 yuan, was borne by Yu Zheng, and he had paid the amount. By this point, the enforcement of the copyright infringement dispute case between Qiong Yao and Yu Zheng, adjudicated by this court, was fully completed. On December 31, 2020, Yu Zheng apologized to Qiong Yao via Weibo.

Relationship Controversy

Qiong Yao's marriage to Ping Xintao has been controversial, with netizens criticizing Qiong Yao for being a homewrecker. In 1963, Qiong Yao submitted her novel "Outside the Window" to "Crown" magazine. The then-president, Ping Xintao, greatly admired it, and they became acquainted, developed a mutual understanding, and began a romantic relationship. In 2017, family conflicts surfaced over the issue of inserting a nasogastric tube for Ping Xintao. Qiong Yao advocated for allowing Ping Xintao to have a peaceful death, but his children, including Ping Yun, angrily criticized Qiong Yao for not visiting for as long as a month. They believed their father's condition was not as dire as Qiong Yao claimed and were unwilling to give up hope for recovery. Qiong Yao ultimately transferred the caregiving rights to them and published the book "Before the Snowflake Falls," exposing the family matters.

33

In 2018, Ping Xintao's ex-wife, Lin Wanzhen, published "Floating Light of the Past," recalling her history with Ping Xintao and Qiong Yao. Lin Wanzhen wrote in the book: "I always thought Xintao was a very upright person and trusted him completely. I never imagined he would have an affair." To facilitate her writing, Qiong Yao moved with her child to the apartment opposite Ping Xintao's home. At that time, Lin Wanzhen gradually noticed the close interactions between Qiong Yao and her husband, Ping Xintao, and later discovered love letters Qiong Yao had written to Ping Xintao. In 1976, Ping Xintao presented a handwritten divorce agreement for Lin Wanzhen to sign, ending the entanglement among the three that had lasted over a decade. In Qiong Yao's writings, the story is told differently.

33

Controversy Over Works

Some of Qiong Yao's works have been criticized by netizens for having "incorrect values" (san guan bu zheng). On the internet, the terms "correct values" (san guan zheng) and "incorrect values" (san guan bu zheng) are widely used and have become important standards for evaluating words and deeds. The emphasis on and judgment of the "values" (san guan) in literary and artistic works is essentially an emphasis on the moral ethics of the works.

35

In most of the works created by Qiong Yao and in her real life, the "love above all else" value is reflected. The pursuit of "love above all else" tends to overlook and even disdain "mundane" values, which is the reason for the criticism from netizens.

34

Estate Distribution

In December 2024, the massive estate left behind by Qiong Yao after her death became a focus of public attention. On December 9, a reporter from Southern Metropolis Daily learned from Qiong Yao's social media account that she had posted in September 2018, mentioning, "The IP in my hands will be handed over to the younger generation, led by Xiu Qiong (Qiong Yao's daughter-in-law)." It is reported that her copyright fees may exceed 4.4 billion New Taiwan dollars (approximately 1 billion Chinese yuan), but their current disposition remains unclear. Staff from the Writers Publishing House told the Southern Metropolis Daily reporter that the company only holds the exclusive publishing rights for the simplified Chinese version of "Qiong Yao's works" in mainland China, and that "the ownership of film and television adaptation rights is unclear."

Qiong Yao (April 20, 1938 – December 4, 2024), born Chen Zhe, was born in Chengdu, Sichuan, with ancestral roots in Hengyang, Hunan. She was a contemporary Chinese writer, screenwriter, and film and television producer.

In 1949, she moved with her parents from mainland China to Taiwan. She began her writing career during her high school years. In 1955, she published the novel Cloud Shadows under the pen name Xin Ru. In 1963, she published her first full-length novel Outside the Window, which brought her fame. In 1964, she published the novel Misty Rain and the story collection Six Dreams, among other works. In 1975, she released the novel By the Water. In 1985, she entered the film and television production industry, and the TV series Several Times the Sunset Glows Red, which she produced, achieved great success. In 1989, she published her autobiography My Story. From 1990 to 1993, TV series she produced, such as Wan Jun and The Plum Blossom Brand, were broadcast. In 1998, the TV series My Fair Princess, for which she wrote the screenplay and served as producer, aired and later won the 17th China TV Golden Eagle Award for Best Long Series. In 2001, the TV series Romance in the Rain, for which she wrote the screenplay and served as producer, was broadcast. In 2018, she compiled and published the Qiong Yao Complete Works. In 2019, she completed the novel Plum Blossom Hero Dream. On December 4, 2024, Qiong Yao passed away at her home at the age of 86.

1

Qiong Yao's creative career spanned multiple fields including novels, essays, and screenplays. Many of her works have been adapted into films and television series, becoming a shared memory for several generations of audiences. In the eyes of readers, Qiong Yao's works are characterized by smooth and elegant prose, intricate and touching stories, and a fresh and romantic atmosphere, filled with a longing for dreams and a persistence in love. Her works are closely integrated with popular culture and are widely circulated on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, Hong Kong, and Macau.

Life Experience

Early Years

On the early morning of April 20, 1938, Qiong Yao was born at the Renji Hospital on Sishengci Street in Chengdu. She lived in Chengdu until she was four years old. In 1942, she moved with her parents back to the ancestral home, "Lanzhi Hall," in Hengyang, Hunan. From the summer of 1944 to the autumn of 1945, under the influence of the War of Resistance Against Japan, she fled with her parents from Hunan to Chongqing. Subsequently, she settled with her mother at the Lu County Lu'nan Middle School in Sichuan. In 1947, she moved with her family to Shanghai and entered school for the first time (Shanghai Sixteenth District National Primary School, today's Hongkou District First Central Primary School). In 1948, she returned to Hengyang with her mother and enrolled at Hengyang Gangzhi Primary School. In the summer of 1949, she moved with her parents to Taipei City, Taiwan Province; in the autumn of the same year, she transferred into the sixth grade at Taipei Normal University Affiliated Primary School. In 1950, she graduated from Taipei Normal University Affiliated Primary School and was admitted to Taipei First Girls' High School.

2

Writing Career

Initial Phase

In 1947, while in primary school, Qiong Yao was deeply inspired by viewing the wall newspapers created by upper-grade students and subsequently became fascinated with writing. She often used the daily conversations between her parents as material, and the content she created frequently made her parents laugh heartily. Soon after, she asked her father to help submit her exercise piece "Poor Little Qing" to the Shanghai-based newspaper "Ta Kung Pao." On December 6, 1947, "Poor Little Qing" was published in the "Modern Children" column on page 9 of "Ta Kung Pao."

2

Qiong Yao's "Poor Little Qing"

![Image 7: December 6, 1947, Ta Kung Pao](https://gbaike-image.cdn.bcebos.com/91529822720e0cf3d7cabba76d1fe51fbe096b637c6f/91529822720e0cf3d7cabba76d1fe51fbe096b637c6f_3_4?x-bce-process=image/format,f_auto)

December 6, 1947, Ta Kung Pao

In 1954, after graduating from junior high school, she was admitted to Taipei Second Girls' High School (now Zhongshan Girls' High School). In her first year of high school, she attempted suicide by taking pills due to poor math grades. In 1955, she published the short story "Cloud Shadows" in the Taiwanese magazine "Morning Light" under the pen name Xin Ru. In 1957, after failing the college entrance exam, she again attempted suicide by taking pills. In July 1958, after failing the college entrance exam a second time, she resolved not to retake the exam and firmly pursued her dream of writing, but several novels she wrote were rejected by publishers. In 1961, she completed the short story "Lover's Valley," which was published in the magazine "Crown."

2

In 1963, drawing from her own experiences, she completed her first full-length novel, "Outside the Window," which was 200,000 characters long. One week after mailing it to the magazine "Crown," she received a letter confirming its publication. It was later published in the "Book of the Month" column of issue 113 of "Crown" magazine. In July, her novella "The Pursuit" was serialized in the supplement of Taiwan's "United Daily News," attracting attention. In September, *Outside the Window* was published as a single-volume book with an initial print run of 1,000 copies. Upon release, it sold out multiple times and was widely praised.

19

Professional Writer

In 1964, she moved to Taipei to settle down and devoted herself to writing. She published three full-length novels, "Misty Rain," "Several Times the Sunset Glows Red," and "Dodder Flower," as well as the collection of novellas and short stories "Six Dreams" and "Lucky Grass."

19

In 1965, she sold the film rights for her novel "Six Dreams" to Taiwan's Central Motion Picture Corporation. Two of the stories, "The Pursuit" and "Mute Wife," were selected for film adaptation. After the films were released, they became very popular. After watching the films in the cinema, Qiong Yao became fascinated with adapting her novels for the screen.

19

In 1966, she published the full-length novels "Purple Shell," "The Boat," and "Cold Mist Green."

3

In 1967, she and Ping Xintao established the Firebird Film Company (which dissolved in 1969). The following year, she adapted the novel "Lucky Grass" to produce the films "Full Moon Over the West Tower" and "Stranger." In 1976, she, along with Ping Xintao and others, established the Giant Star Film Company, which successfully adapted and filmed "Cloud of Romance." In 1983, weary of film production, she decisively closed down the Giant Star Company.

2

In 1985, she and Ping Xintao established the Yiren Communication Company, entering the television industry. They launched the TV series "Several Times the Sunset Glows Red," the first television drama adapted from a Qiong Yao novel, which generated considerable response. The success of "Several Times the Sunset Glows Red" not only led some television stations to adapt other works by Qiong Yao, such as "I Am a Cloud" and "By the Water," but also enabled Taiwanese TV dramas, represented by Qiong Yao's romance dramas, to enter mainland China.

8

In 1988, she visited mainland China for the first time to see relatives, traveling to Beijing, Hubei, Sichuan, Yunnan, and other places, and began compiling her complete works.

2

In January 1989, she published her mainland travelogue "Unbreakable Nostalgia." In May, she returned to Hengyang, Hunan, to pay respects to her ancestors. During this period, she established a cooperative relationship with Hunan Television, actively promoting cross-strait co-production of the TV series "Six Dreams" series, which was completed the following year with "Wan Jun," "Mute Wife," and "Three Flowers," featuring famous cultural landmarks from across the country. In October, she compiled old manuscripts and published her autobiography "My Story," recounting her life story and writing experience.

Personal Life

Family

Qiong Yao's father was Chen Zhiping, a native of Hengyang, Hunan, and a historian. His works include "Lectures on Qin and Han History," "Lectures on Three Kingdoms History," and "General History of China."

30

Qiong Yao's mother was Yuan Xingshu, the eldest daughter of Yuan Lizhen, the eldest son of Liangnan scholar Yuan Xuechang and the renowned female Chinese medicine practitioner and poet Zeng Yi. She was originally from Wujin, Jiangsu, but grew up in Beijing. Hailing from a family of scholars, she was fond of classical literature from a young age and graduated from Beiping (Beijing) Art College.

Romantic Relationships

While in high school, Qiong Yao fell in love with her Chinese literature teacher, who was 25 years her senior and a widower. Later, after failing the university entrance exam, their student-teacher relationship was exposed. Qiong Yao's mother reported their relationship to the "Police Department" and the "Ministry of Education" on the grounds of "seduction of a minor" and "student enticement." The teacher was subsequently dismissed from his school and left Taipei.

7

Qiong Yao's first husband was Ma Senqing. The two married in 1959 and later had a son named Chen Zhongwei. Their marital conflicts deepened following the publication of "*Outside the Window*." In the spring of 1964, they divorced.

2

Qiong Yao's second husband was Ping Xintao. Their relationship began with manuscript solicitations. Over the next few years, they met, got to know each other, co-founded a company, becoming business partners and gradually coming together in their personal lives as well. On May 9, 1979, more than a decade after first meeting, Qiong Yao and Ping Xintao married. Ping Xintao passed away on May 23, 2019.

28

Death

At approximately 13:22 on December 4, 2024, Qiong Yao passed away at her home in Tamsui District, New Taipei City, Taiwan Province. According to her son, Qiong Yao had instructed her secretary, Shu Ling, to check on her at home around noon. The secretary entered the residence and found Qiong Yao had taken her own life in her room. Upon seeing this, the secretary immediately notified emergency services (119). However, when rescue personnel arrived, they found Qiong Yao had no breath or pulse and was clearly deceased, so she was not taken to a hospital. Police from Tamsui arrived at the scene after receiving the report and preliminarily ruled out external interference. Subsequently, Secretary Shu Ling posted Qiong Yao's suicide note and a recitation video titled "When Snowflakes Fall" on behalf of Qiong Yao on Qiong Yao's Facebook fan page. The suicide note mentioned that Qiong Yao had "fluttered away" and hoped the public would not grieve for her. On the same day, following a legal examination by the prosecutor, preliminary results were announced, determining no suspicion of homicide. According to Taiwanese media reports, Qiong Yao died from asphyxiation due to carbon monoxide poisoning.
