Creative Characteristics

Works Mirroring Personal Experience

Starting with Outside the Window in 1963, the romance novels created by Qiong Yao have influenced several generations. The theme of love runs through Qiong Yao's works, but the specific changes in endings and styles highly correspond with her own life experiences. In her early period, Qiong Yao favored tragedies. Her first full-length novel, Outside the Window, was a tragedy. At that time, Qiong Yao had just experienced a fruitless teacher-student romance, which cast a gloomy shadow over her understanding of love. The teacher-student romance depicted in the book bore traces of her own life. Subsequently, Qiong Yao married a husband who also loved writing, but they later separated due to writing, leading to the sentimental and oppressive characteristics evident in her works from this period. After Outside the Window, she successively published novels such as Misty Rain, Six Dreams, Lucky Grass, Several Times the Sunset Glows Red, Dodder Flower, and Sound of the Tide. Most of these works ended in tragedy. In her autobiography My Story, Qiong Yao detailed her decade-long extramarital affair with Ping Xintao. This painful and entangled extramarital relationship became material for her writing, as reflected in works like Purple Shell, I Am a Cloud, and Wave.

In the mid-1970s, during Qiong Yao's middle writing period, she and Ping Xintao, who had been in love for over a decade, finally came together, which had a tremendous impact on her creation. Beginning with Heart Has a Thousand Knots in 1973, Qiong Yao's writing style shifted towards a brighter and more optimistic tone. Although characters still endured many hardships, tragedies were minimized as much as possible, resulting in happy endings. After the 1990s, Princess Pearl maximized the comedic effect. In Qiong Yao's later works, through different characters and love stories, she repeatedly conveyed one viewpoint—"love possesses the power to overcome everything."

32

Meeting the Needs of the Era

Discussing the reasons for the "Qiong Yao fever," some scholars believe that the mid-to-late 1980s coincided with an era of ideological liberation, where sensory entertainment and recreational literature gradually prevailed. The emergence of Qiong Yao's works met the needs of the times. In the 1990s and early 21st century, cultural works diversified, causing Qiong Yao to be temporarily overshadowed. After entering the 21st century, Qiong Yao once again resonated with the modern "light aesthetic era," where literature and film are merely prepared for sensory entertainment and emotional release. Qiong Yao became the spokesperson for the light aesthetic era once more, her trajectory aligning with the era's path from beginning to end. Zhang Yiwu, a professor in the Chinese Department of Peking University, analyzed that in the 1960s, Taiwan was undergoing economic transformation, and people's concepts were changing dramatically, a situation very similar to the changes occurring in mainland China in the 1980s. Qiong Yao's novels had a profound influence on Chinese society at that time. Qiong Yao's works fully express a nostalgia for traditional values as well as an attitude of adapting to the changes of the new era.

32

Describing Emotion Itself

The love in Qiong Yao's works is essentially isolated, stripped of all social attributes. The most classic example is her earlier work Wan Jun. Qiong Yao's romance novels evolved from the Mandarin Duck and Butterfly School of the 1920s and 1930s. The difference is that the love presented in Mandarin Duck and Butterfly School novels was mostly sorrowful, closely related to the overall societal oppression and heaviness. Qiong Yao inherited the "emotion" from the Mandarin Duck and Butterfly School but removed the "sorrow," resulting in an overflowing sentiment. This sentiment does not point to anything; emotion points to emotion itself. In her works, love is both the form and the content. Precisely because Qiong Yao's love stories shed much of their mundane worldly aspects, they have been welcomed by several generations of young people. Descriptions of love triangles and extramarital affairs in Qiong Yao's works serve the need for dramatic construction in the novels; they are matters of novelistic technique.

32

Influence

Unique Literary Model

The love depicted by Qiong Yao is not the love of mortal flesh, but rather a transcendent, otherworldly love akin to that portrayed by Dante in Divina Commedia. The theme of love in Qiong Yao's novels is not grounded in real life but rooted in an ideal kingdom, a point for which she is often criticized. Qiong Yao does not reproduce life as it is, but rather portrays life as it should be. She depicts an ideal world, not stories from real life.

Among the numerous romance writers in Taiwan, Qiong Yao is quite distinctive. Over her decades-long career in writing romance novels, Qiong Yao developed a unique style in terms of characters, themes, structure, language, and other aspects. Her particular life experiences and aesthetic pursuits led her early novels to favor tragedy, while her later works distinctly reject and deconstruct it. Qiong Yao's novels exhibit a tendency toward formulaic patterns in plot structure, characters, themes, and language, forming the distinctive "Qiong Yao model." In the history of modern and contemporary Chinese romance literature, Qiong Yao is a writer who connects the past and the future. On one hand, she inherits the literary traditions of predecessors like Zhang Henshui, while on the other hand, her creative model has influenced contemporary and later writers such as San Mao and Yi Shu.

36

Perfecting the Film System

The significance of Qiong Yao's literary films lies not only in opening up a distinctive tradition of genre films for the development of Taiwanese cinema but also in inheriting the commercial film tradition with strong popular cultural overtones that has been evolving since the birth of Chinese cinema. The emergence, development, and widespread influence of Qiong Yao's films in Chinese communities are, in fact, powerful proof of the shared cultural roots and continuous development across the strait. Qiong Yao's films created a prosperous landscape for Taiwanese cinema, making outstanding contributions to the perfection of its commercial system. This also represents a form of genre shaping during the early stages of Taiwanese film development.

Qiong Yao's films interweave the unique nostalgic consciousness, Chinese complex, and modern concepts of Taiwanese people, presenting a true picture of Taiwanese society. Consequently, Qiong Yao's films possess unique cultural value. This cultural value, combined with the commercial success they achieved at the box office in the 1960s and 1970s, inevitably secures Qiong Yao's films an important place in the history of Taiwanese cinema.

37

Overseas Export of Works

In the 1990s, Princess Pearl caused a sensation in Southeast Asia, Europe, and America, with Vietnam producing a local remake. Foreigners left comments on "C-drama" (Chinese TV drama) forums saying, "When Yi Ping fainted on the stairs, I burst into tears." Foreigners who enjoy C-dramas call themselves Chinenglish Bilingual (Cfan). They follow Chinese TV dramas and variety shows, form interest groups, and critique acting skills. The influence of Chinese TV dramas began to spread overseas, forming an increasingly large overseas fan base for these shows. The "Chinese Wave" is becoming a new force in cultural export.

38

Critical Assessment

In Qiong Yao's works, the characters are not troubled by concerns over food and clothing, and instead are wholeheartedly entangled in matters of emotion. (Comment by writer Wang Anyi)

21

Poetic charm and picturesque beauty are distinguishing features of Qiong Yao's novels. The extensive use of classical poetry, lyrics, and prose endows the originally popular romance fiction with an extraordinary, ethereal elegance. (Comment by Yangcheng Evening News)

22

Although most of the female characters portrayed by Qiong Yao are distinct and possess a sense of independence, some of her views on gender roles remain quite traditional: a woman does not have to be beautiful but must be youthful; a woman who cannot win a man's affection is not a good woman. (Comment by scholar Lin Fangmei)

22

Although, viewed as a whole, the intellectual merit and standard of Qiong Yao's works are uneven, a considerable number of her works possess positive and profound ideological depth. Works such as Misty Rain, Several Times the Sunset Glows Red, and A Red Bean all have commendable aspects in their thematic concerns. For example, Misty Rain integrates marriage and romance into a historical context. Through the rise and fall of the family of Lu Zhenhua, who once dominated much of China, it reflects, from one perspective, decades of turmoil and transformation in Chinese history, and presents a relatively objective depiction of the inevitable trajectory of historical progress. (Comment from A General History of Chinese Literature)

23

Qiong Yao provided a new literary framework for a weak generation, ossifying their thinking and leading them down the path of becoming obedient subjects. (Comment by writer Li Ao)

22

Many of Qiong Yao's novels have been adapted into film and television works, enjoying immense popularity across the Chinese-speaking world. (Comment by Xinhua Net)

73

Several of Qiong Yao's novelistic works have been adapted into widely acclaimed films or television series, including Princess Pearl and A Dream Behind the Curtain, and enjoy great fame in the Chinese-speaking world. (Comment by China Youth Daily)

74

Posthumous Commemoration

On December 4, 2024, the passing of writer Qiong Yao triggered collective mourning from numerous actors who had portrayed roles in her dramas, screenwriters, and celebrities who had collaborated with her. Actors such as Angel, Ma Yili, Tamia Liu, Li Sheng, Brigitte Lin, Qin Lan, Chen Derong, and Ming Jin took to social media, recalling their encounters and collaborative experiences with Qiong Yao, expressing their gratitude and remembrance for her. Simultaneously, Qiong Yao's apprentice, screenwriter Shen Zhining, also shared old photos in tribute.

45

On December 6, 2024, the China Writers Association sent a condolence telegram to the family of Ms. Qiong Yao, expressing grief over her passing and offering condolences to her relatives.

80

On December 7, 2024, at Qiong Yao's ancestral home, Lanzhi Hall, in Hengyang, Hunan, villagers held a memorial activity, braving the rain to bid farewell to Qiong Yao.

79

On December 11, 2024, at a press conference of the Taiwan Affairs Office, spokesperson Zhu Fenglian stated that Ms. Qiong Yao was a highly influential Taiwanese writer who harbored deep affection for the Chinese mainland and played a positive role in promoting cross-strait exchanges and film and television cooperation. We express profound condolences for the passing of Ms. Qiong Yao and extend sincere sympathies to her family.

84

Controversies

Copyright Dispute

On April 20, 2014, Qiong Yao expressed dissatisfaction that Yu Zheng's new drama "Coming Home: The Lost Daughter" plagiarized her earlier work "Plum Blossom Brand." She sent an open letter to the State Administration of Press, Publication, Radio, Film and Television, condemning Yu Zheng's infringement. In May, Qiong Yao filed a lawsuit against Yu Zheng, the screenwriter of "Palace: The Lock Heart Jade," and the production company for infringing the copyright of "Plum Blossom Brand." The case was accepted by the Beijing Third Intermediate People's Court. On December 18, 2015, the final judgment in Qiong Yao's copyright protection case for "Plum Blossom Brand" was delivered. The ruling determined that "Palace: The Lock Heart Jade" infringed upon the adaptation and filming rights of "Plum Blossom Brand." The defendants were ordered to cease the infringement, Yu Zheng was required to apologize to Qiong Yao, and the defendants were to compensate the plaintiff 5 million yuan. In May 2018, because Yu Zheng, who was found liable for infringement, had delayed apologizing to Qiong Yao, the Third Intermediate Court, in accordance with the judgment, published the case details in the "Legal Daily" as an announcement. On May 23, the full cost of this announcement, 336,000 yuan, was borne by Yu Zheng, and he had paid the amount. By this point, the enforcement of the copyright infringement dispute case between Qiong Yao and Yu Zheng, adjudicated by this court, was fully completed. On December 31, 2020, Yu Zheng apologized to Qiong Yao via Weibo.

15

![Image 25: Open Letter](https://gbaike-image.cdn.bcebos.com/9d82d158ccbf6c81e8fb597ebe3eb13532fa4053/9d82d158ccbf6c81e8fb597ebe3eb13532fa4053_url?x-bce-process=image/format,f_auto/resize,m_lfit,h_1024,limit_1)

Open Letter

Relationship Controversy

Qiong Yao's marriage to Ping Xintao has been controversial, with netizens criticizing Qiong Yao for being a homewrecker. In 1963, Qiong Yao submitted her novel "Outside the Window" to "Crown" magazine. The then-president, Ping Xintao, greatly admired it, and they became acquainted, developed a mutual understanding, and began a romantic relationship. In 2017, family conflicts surfaced over the issue of inserting a nasogastric tube for Ping Xintao. Qiong Yao advocated for allowing Ping Xintao to have a peaceful death, but his children, including Ping Yun, angrily criticized Qiong Yao for not visiting for as long as a month. They believed their father's condition was not as dire as Qiong Yao claimed and were unwilling to give up hope for recovery. Qiong Yao ultimately transferred the caregiving rights to them and published the book "Before the Snowflake Falls," exposing the family matters.

33

In 2018, Ping Xintao's ex-wife, Lin Wanzhen, published "Floating Light of the Past," recalling her history with Ping Xintao and Qiong Yao. Lin Wanzhen wrote in the book: "I always thought Xintao was a very upright person and trusted him completely. I never imagined he would have an affair." To facilitate her writing, Qiong Yao moved with her child to the apartment opposite Ping Xintao's home. At that time, Lin Wanzhen gradually noticed the close interactions between Qiong Yao and her husband, Ping Xintao, and later discovered love letters Qiong Yao had written to Ping Xintao. In 1976, Ping Xintao presented a handwritten divorce agreement for Lin Wanzhen to sign, ending the entanglement among the three that had lasted over a decade. In Qiong Yao's writings, the story is told differently.

33

Controversy Over Works

Some of Qiong Yao's works have been criticized by netizens for having "incorrect values" (san guan bu zheng). On the internet, the terms "correct values" (san guan zheng) and "incorrect values" (san guan bu zheng) are widely used and have become important standards for evaluating words and deeds. The emphasis on and judgment of the "values" (san guan) in literary and artistic works is essentially an emphasis on the moral ethics of the works.

35

In most of the works created by Qiong Yao and in her real life, the "love above all else" value is reflected. The pursuit of "love above all else" tends to overlook and even disdain "mundane" values, which is the reason for the criticism from netizens.

34

Estate Distribution

In December 2024, the massive estate left behind by Qiong Yao after her death became a focus of public attention. On December 9, a reporter from Southern Metropolis Daily learned from Qiong Yao's social media account that she had posted in September 2018, mentioning, "The IP in my hands will be handed over to the younger generation, led by Xiu Qiong (Qiong Yao's daughter-in-law)." It is reported that her copyright fees may exceed 4.4 billion New Taiwan dollars (approximately 1 billion Chinese yuan), but their current disposition remains unclear. Staff from the Writers Publishing House told the Southern Metropolis Daily reporter that the company only holds the exclusive publishing rights for the simplified Chinese version of "Qiong Yao's works" in mainland China, and that "the ownership of film and television adaptation rights is unclear."

# Chinese mourn death of Taiwanese romance author

## Chiong Yao was best known to millions via big-budget TV adaptations of her romantic stories.

By Zhu Liye for RFA Mandarin

2024.12.05

![Image 3: Social media sharing button](https://www.rfa.org/pf/resources/static/Social_logos_Share.png?d=164)

![Image 4: Author Chiung Yao poses with her new book at a book release event in Taipei, August 1, 2017.](https://www.rfa.org/resizer/v2/UHL3LOB2MJFGLGUYH6O6L4XKH4.jpg?smart=true&auth=4a9a0ff0ffa3f05f1f02b1a05e388403d20d19efc760a5cc52d4e92535209513&width=1440&height=960)

Author Chiung Yao poses with her new book at a book release event in Taipei, August 1, 2017. (CNA/AFP) 

Viewers in the Chinese-speaking world are mourning the death of Taiwanese romance author Chiong Yao, who took her own life at the age of 86.

Chiong, who was born in the southwestern province of Sichuan with the name Chen Che, and whose family fled to Taiwan at the end of the civil war in 1949, was known to millions of viewers of TV dramas that were adapted from her prolific stream of romantic novels from the 1960s onwards.

Her death in Taipei was reported by China’s state news agency Xinhua, which noted that the news “climbed up to the top trending topic on the popular microblogging site Weibo minutes after it broke.”

“Within an hour or so, more than 1 billion views on relevant posts were recorded by Weibo,” the agency said, using an alternate spelling of her name, Qiong Yao.

Xinhua said that according to the local police and fire department, the writer “was found deceased after taking her own life at her residence.”

Several Chinese media quoted a farewell video from Chiong posted to Facebook in which she says good-bye to her life, and leaves behind her books as her legacy.

“No matter what happened, good or bad, part of me was always chasing the sunrise and sunset, always believing in love and idealism,” she says.

“I don’t want to burden my loved ones with more disease; my heart is at peace.“

![Image 5: Author Chiang Yao meets with Han Kuo-yu while he was Mayor of Kaohsiung, Taiwan, on June 8, 2020.](https://www.rfa.org/resizer/v2/5YUMHL2XGVG2NAKMVG4UJ75BA4.jpg?auth=3723e1f63ef55211ec2da3f91f5b8ef43b6ecf7682afca3fe678570ab8d93245&width=800&height=600)

taiwan-china-romance-novelist-dies-02 Author Chiang Yao meets with Han Kuo-yu while he was Mayor of Kaohsiung, Taiwan, on June 8, 2020. (Kaohsiung City Government) 

Chiong’s passing prompted a massive outpouring of grief on social media, particularly in China, with posts linked to the news trending on Weibo on Wednesday, with readers and viewers hailing her for writing “China’s own Romeo and Juliet,” Xinhua said.

One of Chiong’s works, the Qing Dynasty love story “My Fair Princess,” went on to be adapted into one of the most-viewed Chinese-language TV dramas in history, aired by Hunan TV from 1998-1999.

That novel, along with “Wan Chun” and “Romance in the Rain,” made her into a household name in the Chinese-speaking world.

**Hit on the mainland**

Her novels have long been popular on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, but really took off in China following the economic reforms launched in 1979 by late supreme leader Deng Xiaoping, as an antidote to the political turmoil and violence of the Mao era.

Chinese publishing houses rushed to bring her novels to print in China in the 1980s, with many publishing without her permission.

Luo Xiaohu, editor-in-chief of the Chinese-language Boston Review of Books, said Chiong’s work was “hugely influential.”

“She influenced so many people in the 1980s,” Luo said. “A whole lot of people named their kids after characters in her novel.”

China back then had just seen the end of the Cultural Revolution, Luo said, and Chiong’s novels were a refreshing change from the grand political narratives that had been imposed on cultural works under Mao Zedong’s wife Jiang Qing.

“The generation that came through the Cultural Revolution in China had had no education, no popular literature, and no books in a decade, and Chiong Yao met their needs,” she said.

In Taiwan, her books took off in the wake of the authoritarian repression of pro-democracy activists under the Kuomintang known as the White Terror.

Her novels offered a glimpse of a romantic world in which dreams of love were the main point of being alive.

People who read her work were also listening to romantic Mandarin pop songs from Taiwan and watching kung fu movies from Hong Kong, according to Luo.

A woman who gave only the surname Wu for fear of reprisals said she had been obsessed with “My Fair Princess” as a young girl growing up in China.

“I didn’t even know who Chiong Yao was, but I was obsessed with My Fair Princess,” Wu said. “I would binge more than 10 episodes a day during vacations, and I used to buy stickers, and unauthorized merch like notebooks.”

She said part of the appeal was the show’s light-heartedness, including its slapstick comedy and fight scenes.

“It was hot property,” Wu said.

The show was a turning point for Chiong Yao adaptations, spawning a huge industry that saw many [major Chinese TV stars](https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/broadcast-10292021115517.html "https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/broadcast-10292021115517.html") get their first big break, including Zhao Wei, [Fan Bingbing](https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/apology-10032018111011.html "https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/apology-10032018111011.html") and Wang Yan, who posted messages of mourning and condolence for Chiong on social media.

While her storylines and characters were also criticized for their lack of realism, many read and watched them anyway, because they fulfilled a need for escapist fantasy.

* * *

**RELATED STORIES**

[What do women want? Mandarin pop song lyrics reveal a shift, study shows](https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/china-pop-music-what-women-want-04152024145852.html "https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/china-pop-music-what-women-want-04152024145852.html")

[Bestselling Chinese Martial Arts Fantasy Author Dies in Hong Kong](https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/bestselling-chinese-martial-arts-fantasy-author-dies-10312018123427.html "https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/bestselling-chinese-martial-arts-fantasy-author-dies-10312018123427.html")

[China targets younger Taiwanese with junkets for island’s celebrities](https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/junkets-celebrities-taiwan-06172024112457.html "https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/junkets-celebrities-taiwan-06172024112457.html")

* * *

“Reading Chiong Yao makes you feel much better, because her plotlines for romantic pairings are pretty effortless and brainless,” wrote one reader on social media. “There are often several pairings that play off against each other.”

“They live carefree lives, always have money, and enough leisure time to be happy,” they wrote.

As Chiong herself once explained to Chinese director Shi Shujun: “Some people say my novels and plot lines are unrealistic, but the feelings are real.”

“I think of them as being like a Christmas tree: we know the baubles are manufactured, but they hang their, glittering and shiny, and everyone loves to look at them,” she said.

Given [current military tensions](https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/cia-taiwan-invasion-02032023160341.html "https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/cia-taiwan-invasion-02032023160341.html") in the Taiwan Strait, Chiong’s work also symbolizes a more innocent era in which Taiwanese weren’t constantly aware of the [threat of a Chinese invasion](https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/taiwan-china-invasion-series-07252024045150.html "https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/taiwan-china-invasion-series-07252024045150.html"), and celebrities from both sides of the Strait mingled effortlessly on TV and at award ceremonies, Wu said.

“Her work was able to spread to China because there was a significant increase in economic and cultural exchanges across the Taiwan Strait [in the 1980s and 1990s],” she said. “I don’t think we will be seeing another Chiong Yao for some time to come.”

# Chinese mourn death of Taiwanese romance author

## Chiong Yao was best known to millions via big-budget TV adaptations of her romantic stories.

By Zhu Liye for RFA Mandarin

2024.12.05

![Image 3: Social media sharing button](https://www.rfa.org/pf/resources/static/Social_logos_Share.png?d=164)

![Image 4: Author Chiung Yao poses with her new book at a book release event in Taipei, August 1, 2017.](https://www.rfa.org/resizer/v2/UHL3LOB2MJFGLGUYH6O6L4XKH4.jpg?smart=true&auth=4a9a0ff0ffa3f05f1f02b1a05e388403d20d19efc760a5cc52d4e92535209513&width=1440&height=960)

Author Chiung Yao poses with her new book at a book release event in Taipei, August 1, 2017. (CNA/AFP) 

Viewers in the Chinese-speaking world are mourning the death of Taiwanese romance author Chiong Yao, who took her own life at the age of 86.

Chiong, who was born in the southwestern province of Sichuan with the name Chen Che, and whose family fled to Taiwan at the end of the civil war in 1949, was known to millions of viewers of TV dramas that were adapted from her prolific stream of romantic novels from the 1960s onwards.

Her death in Taipei was reported by China’s state news agency Xinhua, which noted that the news “climbed up to the top trending topic on the popular microblogging site Weibo minutes after it broke.”

“Within an hour or so, more than 1 billion views on relevant posts were recorded by Weibo,” the agency said, using an alternate spelling of her name, Qiong Yao.

Xinhua said that according to the local police and fire department, the writer “was found deceased after taking her own life at her residence.”

Several Chinese media quoted a farewell video from Chiong posted to Facebook in which she says good-bye to her life, and leaves behind her books as her legacy.

“No matter what happened, good or bad, part of me was always chasing the sunrise and sunset, always believing in love and idealism,” she says.

“I don’t want to burden my loved ones with more disease; my heart is at peace.“

![Image 5: Author Chiang Yao meets with Han Kuo-yu while he was Mayor of Kaohsiung, Taiwan, on June 8, 2020.](https://www.rfa.org/resizer/v2/5YUMHL2XGVG2NAKMVG4UJ75BA4.jpg?auth=3723e1f63ef55211ec2da3f91f5b8ef43b6ecf7682afca3fe678570ab8d93245&width=800&height=600)

taiwan-china-romance-novelist-dies-02 Author Chiang Yao meets with Han Kuo-yu while he was Mayor of Kaohsiung, Taiwan, on June 8, 2020. (Kaohsiung City Government) 

Chiong’s passing prompted a massive outpouring of grief on social media, particularly in China, with posts linked to the news trending on Weibo on Wednesday, with readers and viewers hailing her for writing “China’s own Romeo and Juliet,” Xinhua said.

One of Chiong’s works, the Qing Dynasty love story “My Fair Princess,” went on to be adapted into one of the most-viewed Chinese-language TV dramas in history, aired by Hunan TV from 1998-1999.

That novel, along with “Wan Chun” and “Romance in the Rain,” made her into a household name in the Chinese-speaking world.

**Hit on the mainland**

Her novels have long been popular on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, but really took off in China following the economic reforms launched in 1979 by late supreme leader Deng Xiaoping, as an antidote to the political turmoil and violence of the Mao era.

Chinese publishing houses rushed to bring her novels to print in China in the 1980s, with many publishing without her permission.

Luo Xiaohu, editor-in-chief of the Chinese-language Boston Review of Books, said Chiong’s work was “hugely influential.”

“She influenced so many people in the 1980s,” Luo said. “A whole lot of people named their kids after characters in her novel.”

China back then had just seen the end of the Cultural Revolution, Luo said, and Chiong’s novels were a refreshing change from the grand political narratives that had been imposed on cultural works under Mao Zedong’s wife Jiang Qing.

“The generation that came through the Cultural Revolution in China had had no education, no popular literature, and no books in a decade, and Chiong Yao met their needs,” she said.

In Taiwan, her books took off in the wake of the authoritarian repression of pro-democracy activists under the Kuomintang known as the White Terror.

Her novels offered a glimpse of a romantic world in which dreams of love were the main point of being alive.

People who read her work were also listening to romantic Mandarin pop songs from Taiwan and watching kung fu movies from Hong Kong, according to Luo.

A woman who gave only the surname Wu for fear of reprisals said she had been obsessed with “My Fair Princess” as a young girl growing up in China.

“I didn’t even know who Chiong Yao was, but I was obsessed with My Fair Princess,” Wu said. “I would binge more than 10 episodes a day during vacations, and I used to buy stickers, and unauthorized merch like notebooks.”

She said part of the appeal was the show’s light-heartedness, including its slapstick comedy and fight scenes.

“It was hot property,” Wu said.

The show was a turning point for Chiong Yao adaptations, spawning a huge industry that saw many [major Chinese TV stars](https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/broadcast-10292021115517.html "https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/broadcast-10292021115517.html") get their first big break, including Zhao Wei, [Fan Bingbing](https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/apology-10032018111011.html "https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/apology-10032018111011.html") and Wang Yan, who posted messages of mourning and condolence for Chiong on social media.

While her storylines and characters were also criticized for their lack of realism, many read and watched them anyway, because they fulfilled a need for escapist fantasy.

“Reading Chiong Yao makes you feel much better, because her plotlines for romantic pairings are pretty effortless and brainless,” wrote one reader on social media. “There are often several pairings that play off against each other.”

“They live carefree lives, always have money, and enough leisure time to be happy,” they wrote.

As Chiong herself once explained to Chinese director Shi Shujun: “Some people say my novels and plot lines are unrealistic, but the feelings are real.”

“I think of them as being like a Christmas tree: we know the baubles are manufactured, but they hang their, glittering and shiny, and everyone loves to look at them,” she said.

Given [current military tensions](https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/cia-taiwan-invasion-02032023160341.html "https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/cia-taiwan-invasion-02032023160341.html") in the Taiwan Strait, Chiong’s work also symbolizes a more innocent era in which Taiwanese weren’t constantly aware of the [threat of a Chinese invasion](https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/taiwan-china-invasion-series-07252024045150.html "https://www.rfa.org/english/news/china/taiwan-china-invasion-series-07252024045150.html"), and celebrities from both sides of the Strait mingled effortlessly on TV and at award ceremonies, Wu said.

“Her work was able to spread to China because there was a significant increase in economic and cultural exchanges across the Taiwan Strait [in the 1980s and 1990s],” she said. “I don’t think we will be seeing another Chiong Yao for some time to come.”

### Chen Zhongshi, Famed Chinese Author, Dies at 73

Writer of contemporary classic ‘White Deer Plain’ has succumbed to cancer.

[](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?app_id=229302082296247&display=popup&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sixthtone.com%2Fnews%2F796%2Fchen-zhongshi%2C-famed-chinese-author%2C-dies-at-73&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sixthtone.com%2Fnews%2F796%2Fchen-zhongshi%2C-famed-chinese-author%2C-dies-at-73)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Chen%20Zhongshi%2C%20Famed%20Chinese%20Author%2C%20Dies%20at%2073%20@SixthTone;&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sixthtone.com%2Fnews%2F796%2Fchen-zhongshi%2C-famed-chinese-author%2C-dies-at-73)[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sixthtone.com%2Fnews%2F796%2Fchen-zhongshi%2C-famed-chinese-author%2C-dies-at-73)

By [Wu Haiyun](https://www.sixthtone.com/users/21148/wu-haiyun?source=normal_article)

Apr 29, 2016 2-min read [#literature](https://www.sixthtone.com/topics/10175/literature?source=normal_article)[#tradition](https://www.sixthtone.com/topics/10166/tradition?source=normal_article)

Chen Zhongshi, best known for his novel “White Deer Plain,” died on Friday morning at age 73, according to an obituary released by the Writers Association of his native Shaanxi province.

Chen, born in 1942 in Xian, Shaanxi province, northern China, published his first work in 1973, and has more than 30 works to his name. His most influential work is “White Deer Plain,” which he finished in 1993, and which won him the prestigious Mao Dun Literature Prize in 1997.

![Image 7: introduction](https://image5.sixthtone.com/image/0/4/913.jpg)

Chen Zhongshi smokes during a China Writers Association conference in Nantong, Jiangsu province, April 9, 2007. Jiang Jianhua/VCG

“White Deer Plain” describes how two families, the Bais and Lus, live through the changes China faced from the 1840s, the late Qing dynasty, to the 1980s, just after China’s Cultural Revolution. The story incorporates reflections on Chinese national history and traditional culture. A central theme in the book is the decline of agricultural civilization and Confucian tradition over decades of modernization and revolution in China.

![Image 8: newsletter_icon](https://www.sixthtone.com/_next/static/media/newsletter_icon.84026752.png)

The novel was arguably Chen’s greatest work and one of the best-known works of contemporary Chinese literature. Gao Yuanbao, a professor at the department of Chinese language and literary at Fudan University, told Sixth Tone all of Chen’s works are somehow connected to “White Deer Plain.”

The book was also a source of controversy. The judges of the 1997 Mao Dun Literature Prize asked Chen to modify the novel in two places for it to be eligible for the prize. The jury thought Chen misrepresented the Communist revolution and was too explicit in his descriptions of sex. It wasn’t until 15 years later, in 2012, that the unabridged edition came out.

More than 2 million copies of “White Deer Plain” have been published. It has been made into plays and TV series by a number of artists over the past two decades, and in 2011 the movie adaptation won a Silver Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival.

Xiu Xiaolin, a senior editor at the Shanghai Literature and Art Publishing House who befriended Chen Zhongshi more than 30 years ago, told Sixth Tone that Chen said to him before writing “White Deer Plain” that he wanted to create a masterpiece which “he could bring into the coffin as a pillow.”

Chen had been undergoing chemotherapy for tongue cancer, which last year began to spread.

Jia Pingwa, another famous Shaanxi author, told Sixth Tone that he visited Chen on Thursday morning. “At that time, he could not speak but was still conscious, and he was very, very thin,” Jia said. “Chen was a persistent writer who made great contributions to Chinese literature. I am deeply grieved to learn of his death.”

### Chen Zhongshi, Famed Chinese Author, Dies at 73

Writer of contemporary classic ‘White Deer Plain’ has succumbed to cancer.

[](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?app_id=229302082296247&display=popup&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sixthtone.com%2Fnews%2F796%2Fchen-zhongshi%2C-famed-chinese-author%2C-dies-at-73&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sixthtone.com%2Fnews%2F796%2Fchen-zhongshi%2C-famed-chinese-author%2C-dies-at-73)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Chen%20Zhongshi%2C%20Famed%20Chinese%20Author%2C%20Dies%20at%2073%20@SixthTone;&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sixthtone.com%2Fnews%2F796%2Fchen-zhongshi%2C-famed-chinese-author%2C-dies-at-73)[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.sixthtone.com%2Fnews%2F796%2Fchen-zhongshi%2C-famed-chinese-author%2C-dies-at-73)

By [Wu Haiyun](https://www.sixthtone.com/users/21148/wu-haiyun?source=normal_article)

Apr 29, 2016 2-min read [#literature](https://www.sixthtone.com/topics/10175/literature?source=normal_article)[#tradition](https://www.sixthtone.com/topics/10166/tradition?source=normal_article)

Chen Zhongshi, best known for his novel “White Deer Plain,” died on Friday morning at age 73, according to an obituary released by the Writers Association of his native Shaanxi province.

Chen, born in 1942 in Xian, Shaanxi province, northern China, published his first work in 1973, and has more than 30 works to his name. His most influential work is “White Deer Plain,” which he finished in 1993, and which won him the prestigious Mao Dun Literature Prize in 1997.

![Image 7: introduction](https://image5.sixthtone.com/image/0/4/913.jpg)

Chen Zhongshi smokes during a China Writers Association conference in Nantong, Jiangsu province, April 9, 2007. Jiang Jianhua/VCG

“White Deer Plain” describes how two families, the Bais and Lus, live through the changes China faced from the 1840s, the late Qing dynasty, to the 1980s, just after China’s Cultural Revolution. The story incorporates reflections on Chinese national history and traditional culture. A central theme in the book is the decline of agricultural civilization and Confucian tradition over decades of modernization and revolution in China.

![Image 8: newsletter_icon](https://www.sixthtone.com/_next/static/media/newsletter_icon.84026752.png)

The novel was arguably Chen’s greatest work and one of the best-known works of contemporary Chinese literature. Gao Yuanbao, a professor at the department of Chinese language and literary at Fudan University, told Sixth Tone all of Chen’s works are somehow connected to “White Deer Plain.”

The book was also a source of controversy. The judges of the 1997 Mao Dun Literature Prize asked Chen to modify the novel in two places for it to be eligible for the prize. The jury thought Chen misrepresented the Communist revolution and was too explicit in his descriptions of sex. It wasn’t until 15 years later, in 2012, that the unabridged edition came out.

More than 2 million copies of “White Deer Plain” have been published. It has been made into plays and TV series by a number of artists over the past two decades, and in 2011 the movie adaptation won a Silver Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival.

Xiu Xiaolin, a senior editor at the Shanghai Literature and Art Publishing House who befriended Chen Zhongshi more than 30 years ago, told Sixth Tone that Chen said to him before writing “White Deer Plain” that he wanted to create a masterpiece which “he could bring into the coffin as a pillow.”

Chen had been undergoing chemotherapy for tongue cancer, which last year began to spread.

Jia Pingwa, another famous Shaanxi author, told Sixth Tone that he visited Chen on Thursday morning. “At that time, he could not speak but was still conscious, and he was very, very thin,” Jia said. “Chen was a persistent writer who made great contributions to Chinese literature. I am deeply grieved to learn of his death.”

Famed Taiwanese romance novelist Chiung Yao has died in a suspected suicide on Dec 4. She was 86.

According to the local police and fire department, she was found dead at her residence in New Taipei City. Her 63-year-old son from her first marriage reportedly told Taiwanese media that she left a farewell note.

The best-selling writer of popular romance fiction and screenwriter of the hit Chinese drama My Fair Princess (1998 to 2003), which remains a staple of Chinese television via reruns to this day, also left what appears to be a suicide note that was uploaded to Facebook by her secretary.

The 950-word note, structured in stanzas similar to a modern Chinese poem, is dated Dec 3. It came with a pre-recorded video of her dressed in red, with roses in the background.

Chiung Yao was born as Chen Zhe in Chengdu, China, in 1938 and moved to Taiwan with her parents in 1949.

Under her pen name, she became one of the most prolific and successful authors of her generation, whose series of popular romance novels in the 1960s made her a household name. Her works were adapted into films and television dramas that not only kept Sinophone audiences glued to the screens, but also shot well-known stars to fame.

Screen legend Brigitte Lin, now 70, made her debut at the age of 19 in the film Outside The Window (1973), adapted from Chiung Yao’s book of the same name, which depicted a teacher-student relationship inspired by Chiung Yao’s own life.

Her book Fantasies Behind The Pearly Curtain was also made into a 1975 film starring A-listers of the time, such as Hong Kong actor Patrick Tse and Taiwanese actor Charlie Chin.

Chinese stars Zhao Wei and Fan Bingbing, as well as Taiwanese actress-producer Ruby Lin, all gained prominence thanks to My Fair Princess, which starred the trio in its first and second seasons.

Boy band Little Tigers member Alec Su from Taiwan also successfully pivoted to acting with the series, playing one of four main characters. The Qing Dynasty-set show is regarded as one of the most commercially successful Chinese dramas.

Zhao, Su and Ruby Lin also starred in Romance In The Rain (2001), another drama adapted from a Chiung Yao novel.

Zhao posted on Weibo for the first time in three years to mourn Chiung Yao with the words of a Ming Dynasty poem by Yang Shen, about “heroes of mighty feats”.

Ruby Lin also remembered the octogenarian on Weibo. Referring to her on-screen characters, the actress wrote: “To have been your Ziwei (My Fair Princess), Ruping (Romance In The Rain) and Xuehua (Flowers In Fog, 2013) is an honour enough for this lifetime.”

Su said on Weibo that the Chiung Yao works he starred in left an “indelible mark” in his life and that she has left behind “treasures for an era”.

Brigitte Lin reportedly told Taiwanese media that she spoke with Chiung Yao on the phone just months before, and regrets not meeting her in person recently. She called her a strong woman and said she would forever remember her.

Prior to her suicide note, Chiung Yao made a long Facebook post on Nov 28 which hinted at her state of mind. She mourned the loss of her second husband Ping Hsin-tao, who was also her publisher, and wrote of the pain of living without him.

Mr Ping suffered from dementia in his final days and died in 2019. His death was a major blow to Chiung Yao, as she clashed with his children from his first marriage and ex-wife.

She was famously embroiled in a years-long extramarital affair with Mr Ping before he got a divorce, and Mr Ping’s ex-wife published a memoir in 2018 with details about how Chiung Yao interfered with her marriage.

# Best-selling Taiwanese romance writer Chiung Yao dead at 86

Famed Taiwanese romance novelist Chiung Yao has died in a suspected suicide on Dec 4. She was 86.

According to the local police and fire department, she was found dead at her residence in New Taipei City. Her 63-year-old son from her first marriage reportedly told Taiwanese media that she left a farewell note.

The best-selling writer of popular romance fiction and screenwriter of the hit Chinese drama My Fair Princess (1998 to 2003), which remains a staple of Chinese television via reruns to this day, also left what appears to be a suicide note that was uploaded to Facebook by her secretary.

The 950-word note, structured in stanzas similar to a modern Chinese poem, is dated Dec 3. It came with a pre-recorded video of her dressed in red, with roses in the background.

Chiung Yao was born as Chen Zhe in Chengdu, China, in 1938 and moved to Taiwan with her parents in 1949.

Under her pen name, she became one of the most prolific and successful authors of her generation, whose series of popular romance novels in the 1960s made her a household name. Her works were adapted into films and television dramas that not only kept Sinophone audiences glued to the screens, but also shot well-known stars to fame.

Screen legend Brigitte Lin, now 70, made her debut at the age of 19 in the film Outside The Window (1973), adapted from Chiung Yao’s book of the same name, which depicted a teacher-student relationship inspired by Chiung Yao’s own life.

Her book Fantasies Behind The Pearly Curtain was also made into a 1975 film starring A-listers of the time, such as Hong Kong actor Patrick Tse and Taiwanese actor Charlie Chin.

Chinese stars Zhao Wei and Fan Bingbing, as well as Taiwanese actress-producer Ruby Lin, all gained prominence thanks to My Fair Princess, which starred the trio in its first and second seasons.

Boy band Little Tigers member Alec Su from Taiwan also successfully pivoted to acting with the series, playing one of four main characters. The Qing Dynasty-set show is regarded as one of the most commercially successful Chinese dramas.

Zhao, Su and Ruby Lin also starred in Romance In The Rain (2001), another drama adapted from a Chiung Yao novel.

Zhao posted on Weibo for the first time in three years to mourn Chiung Yao with the words of a Ming Dynasty poem by Yang Shen, about “heroes of mighty feats”.

Ruby Lin also remembered the octogenarian on Weibo. Referring to her on-screen characters, the actress wrote: “To have been your Ziwei (My Fair Princess), Ruping (Romance In The Rain) and Xuehua (Flowers In Fog, 2013) is an honour enough for this lifetime.”

Su said on Weibo that the Chiung Yao works he starred in left an “indelible mark” in his life and that she has left behind “treasures for an era”.

Brigitte Lin reportedly told Taiwanese media that she spoke with Chiung Yao on the phone just months before, and regrets not meeting her in person recently. She called her a strong woman and said she would forever remember her.

Prior to her suicide note, Chiung Yao made a long Facebook post on Nov 28 which hinted at her state of mind. She mourned the loss of her second husband Ping Hsin-tao, who was also her publisher, and wrote of the pain of living without him.

Mr Ping suffered from dementia in his final days and died in 2019. His death was a major blow to Chiung Yao, as she clashed with his children from his first marriage and ex-wife.

She was famously embroiled in a years-long extramarital affair with Mr Ping before he got a divorce, and Mr Ping’s ex-wife published a memoir in 2018 with details about how Chiung Yao interfered with her marriage.
