**Chen Che** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters "Traditional Chinese characters"):陳喆; 20 April 1938–4 December 2024), better known by her [pen name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pen_name "Pen name")**Chiung Yao**, was a Taiwanese writer and producer. The name _Chiung Yao_ is taken from the _[Classic of Poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic\_of\_Poetry "Classic of Poetry")_, where it means "splendid pure [jade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jade "Jade")".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-1) Born in [Chengdu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chengdu "Chengdu"), Sichuan, she moved to [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan") with her family in 1949 during the [Chinese civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-2)

A leading figure in Chinese [romance novels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_novel "Romance novel"), she rose to fame with _Outside the Window_ (1963), which led to her association with [Ping Hsin-tao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ping_Hsin-tao "Ping Hsin-tao"), owner of the [_Crown_ magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Culture_Corporation?action=edit&redlink=1 "Crown Culture Corporation (page does not exist)")[[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%9A%87%E5%86%A0%E6%96%87%E5%8C%96 "zh:皇冠文化")]. The two later married and co-founded production companies to adapt Chiung Yao's works for the screen, pioneering [cross-strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-strait_relations "Cross-strait relations") collaboration in television and film.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:9-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-4) Her works achieved enormous popularity across the [Chinese-speaking world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese-speaking_world "Chinese-speaking world") and [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia") in the late 20th century,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:21-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) launching the careers of many actors, with _[My Fair Princess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Fair\_Princess "My Fair Princess")_ ranking among the most-watched Chinese television dramas of all time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:3-7)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Chen Che was born in [Chengdu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chengdu "Chengdu"), China, on 20 April 1938.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:22-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-nytobit-9) She experienced an unstable childhood due to the [Second Sino-Japanese War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Sino-Japanese_War "Second Sino-Japanese War").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:1-10) Her father, [Chen Chih-ping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chen_Chih-ping?action=edit&redlink=1 "Chen Chih-ping (page does not exist)")[[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%99%B3%E8%87%B4%E5%B9%B3 "zh:陳致平")], came from a humble background in [Hengyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengyang "Hengyang"), while her mother, Yuan Hsing-shu, belonged to an upper-class family with roots in [Suzhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzhou "Suzhou") and [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai "Shanghai"); her grandfather was the head of the [Bank of Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Communications "Bank of Communications").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:5-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:6-12) Yuan fell in love with Chen Chih-ping, who was her Chinese teacher, and the two defied social norms and married.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:6-12) When Yuan Hsing-shu became pregnant, Chen Chih-ping, then only 20 years old, initially planned to have the pregnancy terminated. However, upon discovering she was carrying twins—a boy and a girl—he changed his mind and decided to raise the children. The girl was Chiung Yao.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:5-11) During the war, the family endured a turbulent life as refugees. To survive, they performed in plays and sold potatoes, while Chen Chih-ping and Yuan Hsing-shu also taught in various locations, including Guizhou and Sichuan.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:1-10)

With both parents being [Chinese literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_literature "Chinese literature") teachers, the literary atmosphere of her family instilled in her a love for literature from a young age.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:22-8) In 1947, she moved with her family to [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai "Shanghai"), where she published her first short story, _The Poor Little Qing_, on the _[Ta Kung Pao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta\_Kung\_Pao\_(1902%E2%80%931949) "Ta Kung Pao (1902–1949)")_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:32-13) In 1949, her family relocated to Taipei, Taiwan.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:22-8)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:32-13) After arriving in Taiwan, her father became a Chinese literature professor at [National Taiwan Normal University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Taiwan_Normal_University "National Taiwan Normal University"), while her mother worked as a Chinese literature teacher at [Taipei Municipal Chien Kuo High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei_Municipal_Chien_Kuo_High_School "Taipei Municipal Chien Kuo High School").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:19-14) Compared to many of her peers who grew up in post-war Taiwan's poverty, Chiung Yao enjoyed a relatively privileged upbringing.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:42-15) At the age of 14, she published a short story under the pen name Lü Gui. In 1954, she adopted the pen name Xin Ru and published another story.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-16)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:5-11)

Chiung Yao struggled academically as a child, often facing criticism from her parents.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:5-11) In her final year of high school, she fell in love with her Chinese literature teacher, Jiang Ren, who was single and much older than her.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:8-17) The two planned to marry after being admitted to university, but their relationship ended due to opposition from her parents.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:8-17) Ultimately, Chiung Yao did not pass the university entrance exams,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:5-11) and graduated from Taipei Municipal Second Girls' High School (now [Taipei Municipal Zhongshan Girls High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei_Municipal_Zhongshan_Girls_High_School "Taipei Municipal Zhongshan Girls High School")).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:32-13)

In 1959, she married Ma Sen-ching, a graduate of the Foreign Languages Department at National Taiwan University.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-18) Ma worked at Taiwan Aluminium Corporation in [Kaohsiung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaohsiung "Kaohsiung"), where the couple settled after their wedding. In addition to his day job, Ma was a part-time writer.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:11-19) The couple had one son, Chen Chung-wei.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:7-20)

## Career (1964–2013)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career (1964–2013)")]

### Novelist

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Novelist")]

In 1962, Chiung Yao published several short and medium-length stories in _Crown_ magazine.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:16-21) She then rewrote her high school teacher-student romance into the novel _Outside the Window.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung\_Yao#cite\_note-:8-17)_[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) Initially rejected by multiple publishers due to its length, it was eventually accepted for publication by Ping Hsin-tao's _Crown_ magazine.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:9-3)

In July 1963, Chiung Yao's semi-autobiographical love story _Outside the Window_ was serialised in _Crown_ magazine, achieving significant success. It was later released as a standalone book.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:32-13)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) This success led to her acquaintance with [Ping Hsin-tao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ping_Hsin-tao "Ping Hsin-tao").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:9-3) Ping rented a flat opposite his own for Chiung Yao and hired domestic carers, allowing her to focus on writing full-time. As a result, Chiung Yao moved from Kaohsiung to Taipei with her child.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:9-3) Ping's wife, Lin Wan-chen, began to suspect an unusual relationship between Chiung Yao and Ping after their young children told Lin of their conversations.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:9-3)

Chiung Yao's husband, Ma Sen-ching, was deeply humiliated by the public disclosure of her first love and attacked her in newspapers. Their relationship gradually deteriorated.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:10-22) Writer Chi-chi recalled an incident where she visited Chiung Yao's home, and a servant opened the door to find Chiung Yao coming downstairs with bed linens, claiming they were "poisoned" and announcing her intent to divorce Ma Sen-ching.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:11-19) The couple officially divorced in 1964.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:7-20) After the divorce, Chiung Yao and Ping Hsin-tao entered into a romantic relationship.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:11-19) They became a couple on the premiere night of _Outside the Window_ film adaptation, with Chiung Yao becoming Ping's mistress.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:10-22)

Due to the hardships in her personal life, Chiung Yao's early works often had tragic endings. Between 1964 and 1971, her short and medium-length stories explored varied styles.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23) After 1964, Chiung Yao published six bestsellers, including _Fire and Rain_, _Six Dreams_, and _[Many Enchanting Nights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Many\_Enchanting\_Nights?action=edit&redlink=1 "Many Enchanting Nights (page does not exist)")_.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23)

### Film producer

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Film producer")]

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/08/%E3%80%8C%E9%87%91%E9%A6%AC50%E9%A2%A8%E8%8F%AF%E5%B1%95%E3%80%8D%E7%93%8A%E7%91%A4%E7%9A%84%E5%8A%87%E6%9C%AC%E6%89%8B%E7%A8%BF.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%E3%80%8C%E9%87%91%E9%A6%AC50%E9%A2%A8%E8%8F%AF%E5%B1%95%E3%80%8D%E7%93%8A%E7%91%A4%E7%9A%84%E5%8A%87%E6%9C%AC%E6%89%8B%E7%A8%BF.jpg)

[Golden Horse Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Horse_Awards "Golden Horse Awards") 50th Anniversary Exhibition showing Chiung Yao's manuscript _I am a Cloud_.

Between 1964 and 1983, Chiung Yao's works were adapted into 50 films, leading to "Chiung Yao film" becoming a genre in and of itself.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:4-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-25) Chiung Yao's novels and their adaptations sparked a "Chiung Yao fever" in Hong Kong and Taiwan.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23)

#### Authorised adaptations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Authorised adaptations")]

In 1965, Taiwanese director [Li Hsing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Hsing "Li Hsing") adapted two stories from Chiung Yao's _Six Dreams_ into films: _Four Loves_ and _The Silent Wife_. These marked the beginning of cinematic adaptations of Chiung Yao's works.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-26)_Four Loves_ was successful both critically and commercially, while _The Silent Wife_ achieved even greater success, becoming a bestseller in Hong Kong. However, Chiung Yao was occasionally dissatisfied with Li Hsing's adaptations. For example, in _The Silent Wife_, Chiung Yao envisioned the heroine as a "child bride", but Li Hsing insisted on portraying her as a cousin, deviating from the original narrative.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:13-27)

[Shaw Brothers Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaw_Brothers_Studio "Shaw Brothers Studio") in Hong Kong purchased the film rights to her works. Among these, _My Dream Boat_ became the second-highest-grossing Mandarin-language film in Hong Kong that year. After leaving Shaw Brothers, Hong Kong director [Li Han-hsiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Han-hsiang "Li Han-hsiang") founded [Grand Motion Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Motion_Pictures?action=edit&redlink=1 "Grand Motion Pictures (page does not exist)") in Taiwan, where he extensively adapted Chiung Yao's novels for the screen. His film _Many Enchanting Nights_ earned actress Chiang Ching the [Golden Horse Award for Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Horse_Award_for_Best_Actress "Golden Horse Award for Best Actress") for her role as the protagonist.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:13-27)

In the mid-1970s, Li Hsing returned to Chiung Yao's works, adapting _[The Young Ones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Young\_Ones\_(1973\_film) "The Young Ones (1973 film)")_ and _[The Heart has a Million Knots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Heart\_has\_a\_Million\_Knots?action=edit&redlink=1 "The Heart has a Million Knots (page does not exist)")_. These films boosted the popularity of actors [Chen Chen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chen_Chen_(actress) "Chen Chen (actress)") and [Charlie Chin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Chin "Charlie Chin"), who starred in _The Young Ones_. The soundtrack also gained widespread recognition, with [Teresa Teng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teresa_Teng "Teresa Teng")'s renditions of _A Thousand Words_ and _How Can I Leave You_ from the film becoming major hits.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-%E8%98%87%E8%A9%A0%E6%99%BA2018-28)[Brigitte Lin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigitte_Lin "Brigitte Lin"), who had failed her university entrance exams, was discovered by director [Sung Tsun-Shou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sung_Tsun-Shou "Sung Tsun-Shou") from the _Outside the Window_ production team. This marked her entry into the entertainment industry. However, due to copyright disputes, the film was ultimately unable to be released in Taiwan.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:15-29)

#### Superstar Motion Picture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Superstar Motion Picture")]

Unsatisfied with Shaw Brothers' adaptation of _The Purple Shell_,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:13-27) Chiung Yao established Firebird Picture Company in 1966, producing _Mist Over Dream Lake_ and _Lucky Clover_.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:13-27) However, due to poor box office performance, the company closed in 1971.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:14-30) In 1976, Ping Hsin-tao asked his wife Lin Wan-chen for a divorce.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:17-31) That same year, Chiung Yao co-founded Superstar Motion Picture to adapt her novels into films,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:14-30)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:4-24) ending her collaboration with Li Hsing in 1977.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-32)

In 1979, Jiang Ren, the inspiration for the male lead in _Outside the Window_, died, and Chiung Yao married Ping.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:17-31) Chiung Yao and her second husband Ping adapted many of her novels into television series and films, often serving as [producers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_producer "Film producer") or [screenwriters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screenwriter "Screenwriter") themselves.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) Film adaptations in the 1970s often featured [Brigitte Lin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigitte_Lin "Brigitte Lin"), [Joan Lin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Lin "Joan Lin"), [Charlie Chin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Chin "Charlie Chin"), and [Chin Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chin_Han_(actor,_born_1946) "Chin Han (actor, born 1946)"), who were then collectively known as the "Two Lins and Two Chins".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:4-24)

At Superstar, Brigitte Lin became Chiung Yao's go-to actress, starring in many of Chiung Yao's films.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:15-29) Early works such as _Cloud of Romance_ and _The Love Affair of Rainbow_ were scripted by [Chang Yung-hsiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chang_Yung-hsiang "Chang Yung-hsiang"), while later works, including _Moonlight Serenade_ and _Yesterday's Love_, were penned by Chiung Yao herself.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:14-30)_Cloud of Romance_, featuring Brigitte Lin and co-stars Charlie Chin and Chin Han, was a major hit, with the title song sung by [Fong Fei-fei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fong_Fei-fei "Fong Fei-fei") gaining widespread popularity.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:13-27)

Chiung Yao films dominated prime slots during [Lunar New Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_New_Year "Lunar New Year") and [Youth Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_Youth_Day "Taiwan Youth Day").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-33) Songs were often performed by Fong Fei-fei,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-34) with music composed by [Tso Hung-yuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tso_Hung-yuan?action=edit&redlink=1 "Tso Hung-yuan (page does not exist)")[[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%B7%A6%E5%AE%8F%E5%85%83 "zh:左宏元")].[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-35) The films, set in dining rooms and cafes, were nicknamed "[Three-Hall Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-Hall_Films?action=edit&redlink=1 "Three-Hall Films (page does not exist)")[[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E4%B8%89%E5%BB%B3%E9%9B%BB%E5%BD%B1 "zh:三廳電影")]". However, their formulaic nature led to diminishing appeal.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:14-30) After the 1982 failure of _Amid the Rolling Clouds_, Chiung Yao announced her retirement from filmmaking.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-%E8%98%87%E8%A9%A0%E6%99%BA2018-28)

### Television producer

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Television producer")]

#### Adaptations of earlier works

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Adaptations of earlier works")]

Chiung Yao stopped creating film adaptations in 1980, choosing instead to focus on television.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:4-24) From 1982 to 1985, Chiung Yao's writing began to address controversial societal issues, producing works such as _Paradise on Fire_. However, after 1985, she experienced a creative bottleneck and paused her writing until the 1990s.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23) In 1985, Chiung Yao's novels began to be adapted into television dramas. The following year, Chiung Yao and her husband Ping Hsin-tao co-founded Yi Ren Communications.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:16-21) By 1990, four more adaptations were released within a single year. Most of these dramas aired during Taiwan's prime-time evening slots, drawing massive viewership.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23)

#### Romantic melodrama

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Romantic melodrama")]

After Taiwan's lifting of [martial law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_law_in_Taiwan "Martial law in Taiwan"), the society's growing openness and diversity of values led to the decline of the "fighting for love" trope in Chiung Yao's works.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23) Consequently, her stories shifted to settings in late [Qing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty "Qing dynasty") and early [Republican China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%931949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)"), focusing on themes like [class conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_conflict "Class conflict") and [feudal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal "Feudal") restrictions rather than [generational gaps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generational_gap "Generational gap") or romantic disputes.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23) Her works during this period emphasised "love above all" and featured intense melodrama.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:16-21) The female protagonists—dubbed "Chiung Yao Girls"—embodied the image of tragic beauty.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:16-21) While her narratives critiqued feudal patriarchal oppression, they simultaneously portrayed enduring hardship and framed marriage as the ultimate victory.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:16-21)

In 1987, following Taiwan's approval for citizens to visit relatives in China, Chiung Yao travelled there. After Taiwan lifted restrictions on filming in China in 1989, Chiung Yao led her production teams to China, making her the first Taiwanese producer to film on location there. From that point on, nearly all of her television dramas included scenes shot in China, with Chinese actors joining the casts.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:16-21) In the 1990s, her romance-focused dramas resonated with Taiwan's emotionally complex society,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23) while in China, they gained popularity for their themes of freedom and liberation following [years of social suppression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:16-21) In Vietnam, Chiung Yao's works faced initial censorship for their depictions of extramarital affairs and love triangles but regained popularity after the government [embraced reform and openness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C4%90%E1%BB%95i_M%E1%BB%9Bi "Đổi Mới").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:23-36)

#### Romantic comedies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Romantic comedies")]

In 1998, _[My Fair Princess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Fair\_Princess "My Fair Princess")_ marked a significant departure from Chiung Yao's trademark melodramatic style, introducing a light-hearted and comedic tone.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:18-38) This series is "regarded as one of the most popular Chinese-language drama shows of all time".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:3-7) Following this success, Chiung Yao revisited and reimagined her earlier works, producing remakes of her earlier works.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:18-38) In 2013, she released an original drama, _Flowers in Fog_. The series incorporated South Korean influences and contemporary romantic elements to appeal to younger audiences.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-39) However, it received mixed reviews, with some viewers labelling it a "cringeworthy drama".[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-40) Afterward, Chiung Yao gradually withdrew from the entertainment industry.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-41)

## Final years (2014–2024)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Final years (2014–2024)")]

### Copyright lawsuit

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Copyright lawsuit")]

On 15 April 2014, Chiung Yao accused Chinese screenwriter and producer [Yu Zheng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yu_Zheng "Yu Zheng") of blatant [plagiarism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagiarism "Plagiarism"), seeking immediate suspension of the broadcast of his TV series _[Palace 3: The Lost Daughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace\_3:\_The\_Lost\_Daughter "Palace 3: The Lost Daughter")_, which she alleged to have been plagiarized from her 1992 novel _[Plum Blossom Scar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plum\_Blossom\_Scar?action=edit&redlink=1 "Plum Blossom Scar (page does not exist)")[[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%A2%85%E8%8A%B1%E7%83%99 "zh:梅花烙")]_ (梅花烙). Yu denied the claim. On 28 April, Chiung Yao filed a plagiarism lawsuit against Yu.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-42) On 12 December 109 Chinese screenwriters published a joint statement supporting Chiung Yao.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-43) A day later, an additional 30 Chinese screenwriters made their support of Chiung Yao known.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-44)

On 25 December, the court ruled in Chiung Yao's favour, ordering four companies to stop distributing and broadcasting _The Palace: The Lost Daughter_, also demanding Yu Zheng to publicly apologize and pay Chiung Yao [RMB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RMB "RMB") 5 million (around $800,000) in compensation. [China Radio International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Radio_International "China Radio International") called it a "landmark ruling".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-46)

### Family disputes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Family disputes")]

In 1959, Chiung Yao married Ma Sen-ching (馬森慶), also a writer. After she became famous and began to outshine her husband, their marriage broke down and ended in divorce in 1964.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:0-47) In 1979,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:0-47) Chiung Yao married her publisher Ping Hsin-tao, who had had three children with his first wife Lin Wan-zhen. In 2018, Lin published a memoir in which she accused Chiung Yao of breaking up her marriage.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-st-48)

After Ping suffered a stroke and lost nearly all ability to communicate, Chiung Yao had a falling out with her step-children over whether to continue his [intubation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracheal_intubation "Tracheal intubation").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-st-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-49) Thereafter, she became a supporter of voluntary [euthanasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euthanasia "Euthanasia"), as expressed in her open letter published in March 2017.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-50) Ping died on 23 May 2019, at the age of 92.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-51)

### Advocacy for Han Kuo-yu

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Advocacy for Han Kuo-yu")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/1080422%E7%93%8A%E7%91%A4%E5%AE%B4%E6%B5%AA%E6%BC%AB%E9%96%8B%E5%B8%AD%E9%80%9A%E7%A8%BF-04.jpg/250px-1080422%E7%93%8A%E7%91%A4%E5%AE%B4%E6%B5%AA%E6%BC%AB%E9%96%8B%E5%B8%AD%E9%80%9A%E7%A8%BF-04.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1080422%E7%93%8A%E7%91%A4%E5%AE%B4%E6%B5%AA%E6%BC%AB%E9%96%8B%E5%B8%AD%E9%80%9A%E7%A8%BF-04.jpg)

[Han Kuo-yu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Kuo-yu "Han Kuo-yu") and Chiung Yao at a banquet

She refrained from expressing political opinions until 2018 when [Kuomintang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuomintang "Kuomintang") candidate [Han Kuo-yu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Kuo-yu "Han Kuo-yu") won the [Kaohsiung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaohsiung "Kaohsiung")[mayoral election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Taiwanese_local_elections "2018 Taiwanese local elections"). Following his victory, Chiung Yao published an open letter praising him and later accepted an invitation to serve as the chief consultant for Kaohsiung's Love Industry Chain project. In 2020, upon learning of Han's [presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Taiwanese_presidential_election "2020 Taiwanese presidential election"), she once again expressed strong support, referring to him as a "hero" in her writings. After Han's defeat in the election, she posted a message stating: "Though the people may shed tears, the hero remains unyielding. After the heart-wrenching pain, may the scars heal".[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-52)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Death")]

On 4 December 2024, Chiung Yao was found dead at her home in Tamsui District, New Taipei City, after an apparent [charcoal-burning suicide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charcoal-burning_suicide "Charcoal-burning suicide"), and left behind a note.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-53) Her son stated that he had asked her secretary to check on her around midday. Upon entering the house, the secretary discovered that Chiung Yao had no vital signs and immediately called emergency services. When paramedics arrived, they confirmed she had died and did not transport her to the hospital.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:02-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-z235-55) Local police confirmed that there was no external intervention in her death.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:2-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-58) She died at the age of 86.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:2-57)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-59)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:3-7)

Six days before her death, Chiung Yao had posted a tribute to her late husband on social media.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-60) In her suicide note, she described her death as "flitting away",[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-61) and wrote, "I have truly lived, never wasted my life".[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-62) Later that afternoon, her secretary posted a pre-recorded video and her final written work, _When Snowflakes Fall_, on Chiung Yao's Facebook page.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-65) In her final social media message, she expressed a desire to avoid the pain of "weakness, deterioration, illness, hospital visits, treatment, and lingering suffering". However, she also urged younger generations not to give up on life easily.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-66) Many actors who had starred in her works, such as [Zhao Wei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhao_Wei "Zhao Wei"), expressed their condolences online.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-67)

Her death also sparked discussions in Taiwan about euthanasia.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-68) On 5 December, Chiung Yao's family announced on Facebook that, as per her last will, no public commemorations would be held, in order to avoid using public resources.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-69)

Chinese dissident [Wang Dan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Dan_(dissident) "Wang Dan (dissident)") expressed disapproval of Chiung Yao's later political stance but urged respect for others' choices to mourn or not mourn her death. He emphasised that "not everything in this world needs to be measured by [political correctness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_correctness "Political correctness")".[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-70)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Reception")]

Chiung Yao's romance novels were very well received in Taiwan, and by the 1990s, she was also one of the best-selling authors in China.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:21-5) She has since been enormously popular throughout the Chinese-speaking world.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) Chiung Yao's readership and viewership are predominantly female, owing to her emphasis on the feelings of young women.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-71) Her biggest sellers are _Outside the Window_ and _Deep Is the Courtyard_ (1969), which have been repeatedly reprinted.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) She is often regarded as among the most popular and foremost contemporary romance novelists in the Chinese-speaking world.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-72)

Her novels have been praised for the [prose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prose "Prose"), the poetry that is part of her earlier works, and the literary allusions of their titles.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) The Columbia Companion to Modern East Asian Literature states the novels are sometimes described as "morbid", as some feature socially or ethically questionable romantic relationships (e.g. between teacher and student).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) Her romance novels and their film adaptions have been criticized for their [melodramatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melodrama "Melodrama")[plotlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plotline "Plotline")[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-74) and long-winded dialogues.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-75)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Personal life")]

### Family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Family")]

Chiung Yao's second husband was Ping Hsin-tao, the head of Crown Publishing, with whom she had an eight-year extramarital affair before their marriage.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-z235-55) Her father, Chen Chih-ping, was a professor in the Department of Chinese Literature at National Taiwan Normal University.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:19-14) Her mother, Yuan Hsing-shu, taught Chinese at [Taipei Municipal Chien Kuo High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei_Municipal_Chien_Kuo_High_School "Taipei Municipal Chien Kuo High School").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:19-14) Her maternal grandfather, Yuan Li-chen, served as the first president of the Bank of Communications.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:6-12) Her maternal grandmother, Tseng Yi, was self-taught and excelled in poetry and painting. She was also a nationally renowned female physician in China.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:6-12) Her granduncle, [Yuan Li-zhun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_Li-zhun?action=edit&redlink=1 "Yuan Li-zhun (page does not exist)")[[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%A2%81%E5%8B%B5%E6%BA%96 "zh:袁勵準")], was a tutor to the [Xuantong Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xuantong_Emperor "Xuantong Emperor").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:6-12) Her aunt, [Yuan Jing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_Jing_(writer) "Yuan Jing (writer)"), was a writer, and another aunt, [Yuan Xiaoyuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_Xiaoyuan "Yuan Xiaoyuan"), was China's first female diplomat and tax official.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:6-12)

### Religion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Religion")]

Chiung Yao was an [atheist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atheism "Atheism"). In her later years, she expressed respect for religion on multiple occasions but consistently rejected any form of [proselytisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proselytism "Proselytism") or religious rituals. She regarded ghosts and deities as elements of literature and drama and rejected the possibility of their existence in reality. She advocated confronting life by enriching oneself rather than relying on religion or [superstitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superstition "Superstition").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:20-76)

In her will, she explicitly requested that no religious practices be used to commemorate her - such as setting up a mourning hall, burning [joss paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_paper "Joss paper"), or holding traditional rituals like the "seven-day rites". Instead, she expressed a preference for an [eco-friendly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eco-friendly "Eco-friendly") flower burial. She emphasized that death was a deeply personal matter and should not impose a burden on others.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:20-76)

**Chen Che** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters "Traditional Chinese characters"):陳喆; 20 April 1938–4 December 2024), better known by her [pen name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pen_name "Pen name")**Chiung Yao**, was a Taiwanese writer and producer. The name _Chiung Yao_ is taken from the _[Classic of Poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic\_of\_Poetry "Classic of Poetry")_, where it means "splendid pure [jade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jade "Jade")".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-1) Born in [Chengdu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chengdu "Chengdu"), Sichuan, she moved to [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan") with her family in 1949 during the [Chinese civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-2)

A leading figure in Chinese [romance novels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_novel "Romance novel"), she rose to fame with _Outside the Window_ (1963), which led to her association with [Ping Hsin-tao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ping_Hsin-tao "Ping Hsin-tao"), owner of the [_Crown_ magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Culture_Corporation?action=edit&redlink=1 "Crown Culture Corporation (page does not exist)")[[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%9A%87%E5%86%A0%E6%96%87%E5%8C%96 "zh:皇冠文化")]. The two later married and co-founded production companies to adapt Chiung Yao's works for the screen, pioneering [cross-strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-strait_relations "Cross-strait relations") collaboration in television and film.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:9-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-4) Her works achieved enormous popularity across the [Chinese-speaking world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese-speaking_world "Chinese-speaking world") and [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia") in the late 20th century,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:21-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) launching the careers of many actors, with _[My Fair Princess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Fair\_Princess "My Fair Princess")_ ranking among the most-watched Chinese television dramas of all time.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:3-7)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Chen Che was born in [Chengdu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chengdu "Chengdu"), China, on 20 April 1938.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:22-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-nytobit-9) She experienced an unstable childhood due to the [Second Sino-Japanese War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Sino-Japanese_War "Second Sino-Japanese War").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:1-10) Her father, [Chen Chih-ping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chen_Chih-ping?action=edit&redlink=1 "Chen Chih-ping (page does not exist)")[[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%99%B3%E8%87%B4%E5%B9%B3 "zh:陳致平")], came from a humble background in [Hengyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengyang "Hengyang"), while her mother, Yuan Hsing-shu, belonged to an upper-class family with roots in [Suzhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzhou "Suzhou") and [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai "Shanghai"); her grandfather was the head of the [Bank of Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_Communications "Bank of Communications").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:5-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:6-12) Yuan fell in love with Chen Chih-ping, who was her Chinese teacher, and the two defied social norms and married.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:6-12) When Yuan Hsing-shu became pregnant, Chen Chih-ping, then only 20 years old, initially planned to have the pregnancy terminated. However, upon discovering she was carrying twins—a boy and a girl—he changed his mind and decided to raise the children. The girl was Chiung Yao.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:5-11) During the war, the family endured a turbulent life as refugees. To survive, they performed in plays and sold potatoes, while Chen Chih-ping and Yuan Hsing-shu also taught in various locations, including Guizhou and Sichuan.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:1-10)

With both parents being [Chinese literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_literature "Chinese literature") teachers, the literary atmosphere of her family instilled in her a love for literature from a young age.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:22-8) In 1947, she moved with her family to [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai "Shanghai"), where she published her first short story, _The Poor Little Qing_, on the _[Ta Kung Pao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ta\_Kung\_Pao\_(1902%E2%80%931949) "Ta Kung Pao (1902–1949)")_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:32-13) In 1949, her family relocated to Taipei, Taiwan.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:22-8)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:32-13) After arriving in Taiwan, her father became a Chinese literature professor at [National Taiwan Normal University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Taiwan_Normal_University "National Taiwan Normal University"), while her mother worked as a Chinese literature teacher at [Taipei Municipal Chien Kuo High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei_Municipal_Chien_Kuo_High_School "Taipei Municipal Chien Kuo High School").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:19-14) Compared to many of her peers who grew up in post-war Taiwan's poverty, Chiung Yao enjoyed a relatively privileged upbringing.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:42-15) At the age of 14, she published a short story under the pen name Lü Gui. In 1954, she adopted the pen name Xin Ru and published another story.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-16)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:5-11)

Chiung Yao struggled academically as a child, often facing criticism from her parents.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:5-11) In her final year of high school, she fell in love with her Chinese literature teacher, Jiang Ren, who was single and much older than her.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:8-17) The two planned to marry after being admitted to university, but their relationship ended due to opposition from her parents.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:8-17) Ultimately, Chiung Yao did not pass the university entrance exams,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:5-11) and graduated from Taipei Municipal Second Girls' High School (now [Taipei Municipal Zhongshan Girls High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei_Municipal_Zhongshan_Girls_High_School "Taipei Municipal Zhongshan Girls High School")).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:32-13)

In 1959, she married Ma Sen-ching, a graduate of the Foreign Languages Department at National Taiwan University.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-18) Ma worked at Taiwan Aluminium Corporation in [Kaohsiung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaohsiung "Kaohsiung"), where the couple settled after their wedding. In addition to his day job, Ma was a part-time writer.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:11-19) The couple had one son, Chen Chung-wei.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:7-20)

## Career (1964–2013)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career (1964–2013)")]

### Novelist

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Novelist")]

In 1962, Chiung Yao published several short and medium-length stories in _Crown_ magazine.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:16-21) She then rewrote her high school teacher-student romance into the novel _Outside the Window.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung\_Yao#cite\_note-:8-17)_[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) Initially rejected by multiple publishers due to its length, it was eventually accepted for publication by Ping Hsin-tao's _Crown_ magazine.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:9-3)

In July 1963, Chiung Yao's semi-autobiographical love story _Outside the Window_ was serialised in _Crown_ magazine, achieving significant success. It was later released as a standalone book.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:32-13)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) This success led to her acquaintance with [Ping Hsin-tao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ping_Hsin-tao "Ping Hsin-tao").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:9-3) Ping rented a flat opposite his own for Chiung Yao and hired domestic carers, allowing her to focus on writing full-time. As a result, Chiung Yao moved from Kaohsiung to Taipei with her child.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:9-3) Ping's wife, Lin Wan-chen, began to suspect an unusual relationship between Chiung Yao and Ping after their young children told Lin of their conversations.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:9-3)

Chiung Yao's husband, Ma Sen-ching, was deeply humiliated by the public disclosure of her first love and attacked her in newspapers. Their relationship gradually deteriorated.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:10-22) Writer Chi-chi recalled an incident where she visited Chiung Yao's home, and a servant opened the door to find Chiung Yao coming downstairs with bed linens, claiming they were "poisoned" and announcing her intent to divorce Ma Sen-ching.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:11-19) The couple officially divorced in 1964.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:7-20) After the divorce, Chiung Yao and Ping Hsin-tao entered into a romantic relationship.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:11-19) They became a couple on the premiere night of _Outside the Window_ film adaptation, with Chiung Yao becoming Ping's mistress.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:10-22)

Due to the hardships in her personal life, Chiung Yao's early works often had tragic endings. Between 1964 and 1971, her short and medium-length stories explored varied styles.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23) After 1964, Chiung Yao published six bestsellers, including _Fire and Rain_, _Six Dreams_, and _[Many Enchanting Nights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Many\_Enchanting\_Nights?action=edit&redlink=1 "Many Enchanting Nights (page does not exist)")_.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23)

### Film producer

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Film producer")]

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/08/%E3%80%8C%E9%87%91%E9%A6%AC50%E9%A2%A8%E8%8F%AF%E5%B1%95%E3%80%8D%E7%93%8A%E7%91%A4%E7%9A%84%E5%8A%87%E6%9C%AC%E6%89%8B%E7%A8%BF.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%E3%80%8C%E9%87%91%E9%A6%AC50%E9%A2%A8%E8%8F%AF%E5%B1%95%E3%80%8D%E7%93%8A%E7%91%A4%E7%9A%84%E5%8A%87%E6%9C%AC%E6%89%8B%E7%A8%BF.jpg)

[Golden Horse Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Horse_Awards "Golden Horse Awards") 50th Anniversary Exhibition showing Chiung Yao's manuscript _I am a Cloud_.

Between 1964 and 1983, Chiung Yao's works were adapted into 50 films, leading to "Chiung Yao film" becoming a genre in and of itself.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:4-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-25) Chiung Yao's novels and their adaptations sparked a "Chiung Yao fever" in Hong Kong and Taiwan.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23)

#### Authorised adaptations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Authorised adaptations")]

In 1965, Taiwanese director [Li Hsing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Hsing "Li Hsing") adapted two stories from Chiung Yao's _Six Dreams_ into films: _Four Loves_ and _The Silent Wife_. These marked the beginning of cinematic adaptations of Chiung Yao's works.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-26)_Four Loves_ was successful both critically and commercially, while _The Silent Wife_ achieved even greater success, becoming a bestseller in Hong Kong. However, Chiung Yao was occasionally dissatisfied with Li Hsing's adaptations. For example, in _The Silent Wife_, Chiung Yao envisioned the heroine as a "child bride", but Li Hsing insisted on portraying her as a cousin, deviating from the original narrative.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:13-27)

[Shaw Brothers Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaw_Brothers_Studio "Shaw Brothers Studio") in Hong Kong purchased the film rights to her works. Among these, _My Dream Boat_ became the second-highest-grossing Mandarin-language film in Hong Kong that year. After leaving Shaw Brothers, Hong Kong director [Li Han-hsiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Han-hsiang "Li Han-hsiang") founded [Grand Motion Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Motion_Pictures?action=edit&redlink=1 "Grand Motion Pictures (page does not exist)") in Taiwan, where he extensively adapted Chiung Yao's novels for the screen. His film _Many Enchanting Nights_ earned actress Chiang Ching the [Golden Horse Award for Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Horse_Award_for_Best_Actress "Golden Horse Award for Best Actress") for her role as the protagonist.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:13-27)

In the mid-1970s, Li Hsing returned to Chiung Yao's works, adapting _[The Young Ones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Young\_Ones\_(1973\_film) "The Young Ones (1973 film)")_ and _[The Heart has a Million Knots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Heart\_has\_a\_Million\_Knots?action=edit&redlink=1 "The Heart has a Million Knots (page does not exist)")_. These films boosted the popularity of actors [Chen Chen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chen_Chen_(actress) "Chen Chen (actress)") and [Charlie Chin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Chin "Charlie Chin"), who starred in _The Young Ones_. The soundtrack also gained widespread recognition, with [Teresa Teng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teresa_Teng "Teresa Teng")'s renditions of _A Thousand Words_ and _How Can I Leave You_ from the film becoming major hits.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-%E8%98%87%E8%A9%A0%E6%99%BA2018-28)[Brigitte Lin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigitte_Lin "Brigitte Lin"), who had failed her university entrance exams, was discovered by director [Sung Tsun-Shou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sung_Tsun-Shou "Sung Tsun-Shou") from the _Outside the Window_ production team. This marked her entry into the entertainment industry. However, due to copyright disputes, the film was ultimately unable to be released in Taiwan.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:15-29)

#### Superstar Motion Picture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Superstar Motion Picture")]

Unsatisfied with Shaw Brothers' adaptation of _The Purple Shell_,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:13-27) Chiung Yao established Firebird Picture Company in 1966, producing _Mist Over Dream Lake_ and _Lucky Clover_.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:13-27) However, due to poor box office performance, the company closed in 1971.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:14-30) In 1976, Ping Hsin-tao asked his wife Lin Wan-chen for a divorce.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:17-31) That same year, Chiung Yao co-founded Superstar Motion Picture to adapt her novels into films,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:14-30)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:4-24) ending her collaboration with Li Hsing in 1977.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-32)

In 1979, Jiang Ren, the inspiration for the male lead in _Outside the Window_, died, and Chiung Yao married Ping.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:17-31) Chiung Yao and her second husband Ping adapted many of her novels into television series and films, often serving as [producers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_producer "Film producer") or [screenwriters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screenwriter "Screenwriter") themselves.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) Film adaptations in the 1970s often featured [Brigitte Lin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigitte_Lin "Brigitte Lin"), [Joan Lin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Lin "Joan Lin"), [Charlie Chin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Chin "Charlie Chin"), and [Chin Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chin_Han_(actor,_born_1946) "Chin Han (actor, born 1946)"), who were then collectively known as the "Two Lins and Two Chins".[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:4-24)

At Superstar, Brigitte Lin became Chiung Yao's go-to actress, starring in many of Chiung Yao's films.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:15-29) Early works such as _Cloud of Romance_ and _The Love Affair of Rainbow_ were scripted by [Chang Yung-hsiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chang_Yung-hsiang "Chang Yung-hsiang"), while later works, including _Moonlight Serenade_ and _Yesterday's Love_, were penned by Chiung Yao herself.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:14-30)_Cloud of Romance_, featuring Brigitte Lin and co-stars Charlie Chin and Chin Han, was a major hit, with the title song sung by [Fong Fei-fei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fong_Fei-fei "Fong Fei-fei") gaining widespread popularity.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:13-27)

Chiung Yao films dominated prime slots during [Lunar New Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_New_Year "Lunar New Year") and [Youth Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_Youth_Day "Taiwan Youth Day").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-33) Songs were often performed by Fong Fei-fei,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-34) with music composed by [Tso Hung-yuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tso_Hung-yuan?action=edit&redlink=1 "Tso Hung-yuan (page does not exist)")[[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%B7%A6%E5%AE%8F%E5%85%83 "zh:左宏元")].[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-35) The films, set in dining rooms and cafes, were nicknamed "[Three-Hall Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-Hall_Films?action=edit&redlink=1 "Three-Hall Films (page does not exist)")[[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E4%B8%89%E5%BB%B3%E9%9B%BB%E5%BD%B1 "zh:三廳電影")]". However, their formulaic nature led to diminishing appeal.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:14-30) After the 1982 failure of _Amid the Rolling Clouds_, Chiung Yao announced her retirement from filmmaking.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-%E8%98%87%E8%A9%A0%E6%99%BA2018-28)

### Television producer

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Television producer")]

#### Adaptations of earlier works

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Adaptations of earlier works")]

Chiung Yao stopped creating film adaptations in 1980, choosing instead to focus on television.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:4-24) From 1982 to 1985, Chiung Yao's writing began to address controversial societal issues, producing works such as _Paradise on Fire_. However, after 1985, she experienced a creative bottleneck and paused her writing until the 1990s.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23) In 1985, Chiung Yao's novels began to be adapted into television dramas. The following year, Chiung Yao and her husband Ping Hsin-tao co-founded Yi Ren Communications.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:16-21) By 1990, four more adaptations were released within a single year. Most of these dramas aired during Taiwan's prime-time evening slots, drawing massive viewership.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23)

#### Romantic melodrama

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Romantic melodrama")]

After Taiwan's lifting of [martial law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_law_in_Taiwan "Martial law in Taiwan"), the society's growing openness and diversity of values led to the decline of the "fighting for love" trope in Chiung Yao's works.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23) Consequently, her stories shifted to settings in late [Qing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_dynasty "Qing dynasty") and early [Republican China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%931949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)"), focusing on themes like [class conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_conflict "Class conflict") and [feudal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal "Feudal") restrictions rather than [generational gaps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generational_gap "Generational gap") or romantic disputes.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23) Her works during this period emphasised "love above all" and featured intense melodrama.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:16-21) The female protagonists—dubbed "Chiung Yao Girls"—embodied the image of tragic beauty.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:16-21) While her narratives critiqued feudal patriarchal oppression, they simultaneously portrayed enduring hardship and framed marriage as the ultimate victory.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:16-21)

In 1987, following Taiwan's approval for citizens to visit relatives in China, Chiung Yao travelled there. After Taiwan lifted restrictions on filming in China in 1989, Chiung Yao led her production teams to China, making her the first Taiwanese producer to film on location there. From that point on, nearly all of her television dramas included scenes shot in China, with Chinese actors joining the casts.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:16-21) In the 1990s, her romance-focused dramas resonated with Taiwan's emotionally complex society,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:12-23) while in China, they gained popularity for their themes of freedom and liberation following [years of social suppression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:16-21) In Vietnam, Chiung Yao's works faced initial censorship for their depictions of extramarital affairs and love triangles but regained popularity after the government [embraced reform and openness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C4%90%E1%BB%95i_M%E1%BB%9Bi "Đổi Mới").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:23-36)

#### Romantic comedies

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Romantic comedies")]

In 1998, _[My Fair Princess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Fair\_Princess "My Fair Princess")_ marked a significant departure from Chiung Yao's trademark melodramatic style, introducing a light-hearted and comedic tone.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:18-38) This series is "regarded as one of the most popular Chinese-language drama shows of all time".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:3-7) Following this success, Chiung Yao revisited and reimagined her earlier works, producing remakes of her earlier works.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:18-38) In 2013, she released an original drama, _Flowers in Fog_. The series incorporated South Korean influences and contemporary romantic elements to appeal to younger audiences.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-39) However, it received mixed reviews, with some viewers labelling it a "cringeworthy drama".[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-40) Afterward, Chiung Yao gradually withdrew from the entertainment industry.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-41)

## Final years (2014–2024)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Final years (2014–2024)")]

### Copyright lawsuit

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Copyright lawsuit")]

On 15 April 2014, Chiung Yao accused Chinese screenwriter and producer [Yu Zheng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yu_Zheng "Yu Zheng") of blatant [plagiarism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagiarism "Plagiarism"), seeking immediate suspension of the broadcast of his TV series _[Palace 3: The Lost Daughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace\_3:\_The\_Lost\_Daughter "Palace 3: The Lost Daughter")_, which she alleged to have been plagiarized from her 1992 novel _[Plum Blossom Scar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plum\_Blossom\_Scar?action=edit&redlink=1 "Plum Blossom Scar (page does not exist)")[[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%A2%85%E8%8A%B1%E7%83%99 "zh:梅花烙")]_ (梅花烙). Yu denied the claim. On 28 April, Chiung Yao filed a plagiarism lawsuit against Yu.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-42) On 12 December 109 Chinese screenwriters published a joint statement supporting Chiung Yao.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-43) A day later, an additional 30 Chinese screenwriters made their support of Chiung Yao known.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-44)

On 25 December, the court ruled in Chiung Yao's favour, ordering four companies to stop distributing and broadcasting _The Palace: The Lost Daughter_, also demanding Yu Zheng to publicly apologize and pay Chiung Yao [RMB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RMB "RMB") 5 million (around $800,000) in compensation. [China Radio International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Radio_International "China Radio International") called it a "landmark ruling".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-46)

### Family disputes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Family disputes")]

In 1959, Chiung Yao married Ma Sen-ching (馬森慶), also a writer. After she became famous and began to outshine her husband, their marriage broke down and ended in divorce in 1964.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:0-47) In 1979,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:0-47) Chiung Yao married her publisher Ping Hsin-tao, who had had three children with his first wife Lin Wan-zhen. In 2018, Lin published a memoir in which she accused Chiung Yao of breaking up her marriage.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-st-48)

After Ping suffered a stroke and lost nearly all ability to communicate, Chiung Yao had a falling out with her step-children over whether to continue his [intubation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracheal_intubation "Tracheal intubation").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-st-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-49) Thereafter, she became a supporter of voluntary [euthanasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euthanasia "Euthanasia"), as expressed in her open letter published in March 2017.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-50) Ping died on 23 May 2019, at the age of 92.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-51)

### Advocacy for Han Kuo-yu

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Advocacy for Han Kuo-yu")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/1080422%E7%93%8A%E7%91%A4%E5%AE%B4%E6%B5%AA%E6%BC%AB%E9%96%8B%E5%B8%AD%E9%80%9A%E7%A8%BF-04.jpg/250px-1080422%E7%93%8A%E7%91%A4%E5%AE%B4%E6%B5%AA%E6%BC%AB%E9%96%8B%E5%B8%AD%E9%80%9A%E7%A8%BF-04.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1080422%E7%93%8A%E7%91%A4%E5%AE%B4%E6%B5%AA%E6%BC%AB%E9%96%8B%E5%B8%AD%E9%80%9A%E7%A8%BF-04.jpg)

[Han Kuo-yu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Kuo-yu "Han Kuo-yu") and Chiung Yao at a banquet

She refrained from expressing political opinions until 2018 when [Kuomintang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuomintang "Kuomintang") candidate [Han Kuo-yu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Kuo-yu "Han Kuo-yu") won the [Kaohsiung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaohsiung "Kaohsiung")[mayoral election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Taiwanese_local_elections "2018 Taiwanese local elections"). Following his victory, Chiung Yao published an open letter praising him and later accepted an invitation to serve as the chief consultant for Kaohsiung's Love Industry Chain project. In 2020, upon learning of Han's [presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Taiwanese_presidential_election "2020 Taiwanese presidential election"), she once again expressed strong support, referring to him as a "hero" in her writings. After Han's defeat in the election, she posted a message stating: "Though the people may shed tears, the hero remains unyielding. After the heart-wrenching pain, may the scars heal".[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-52)

## Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Death")]

On 4 December 2024, Chiung Yao was found dead at her home in Tamsui District, New Taipei City, after an apparent [charcoal-burning suicide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charcoal-burning_suicide "Charcoal-burning suicide"), and left behind a note.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-53) Her son stated that he had asked her secretary to check on her around midday. Upon entering the house, the secretary discovered that Chiung Yao had no vital signs and immediately called emergency services. When paramedics arrived, they confirmed she had died and did not transport her to the hospital.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:02-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-z235-55) Local police confirmed that there was no external intervention in her death.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:2-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-58) She died at the age of 86.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:2-57)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-59)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:3-7)

Six days before her death, Chiung Yao had posted a tribute to her late husband on social media.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-60) In her suicide note, she described her death as "flitting away",[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-61) and wrote, "I have truly lived, never wasted my life".[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-62) Later that afternoon, her secretary posted a pre-recorded video and her final written work, _When Snowflakes Fall_, on Chiung Yao's Facebook page.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-65) In her final social media message, she expressed a desire to avoid the pain of "weakness, deterioration, illness, hospital visits, treatment, and lingering suffering". However, she also urged younger generations not to give up on life easily.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-66) Many actors who had starred in her works, such as [Zhao Wei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhao_Wei "Zhao Wei"), expressed their condolences online.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-67)

Her death also sparked discussions in Taiwan about euthanasia.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-68) On 5 December, Chiung Yao's family announced on Facebook that, as per her last will, no public commemorations would be held, in order to avoid using public resources.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-69)

Chinese dissident [Wang Dan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Dan_(dissident) "Wang Dan (dissident)") expressed disapproval of Chiung Yao's later political stance but urged respect for others' choices to mourn or not mourn her death. He emphasised that "not everything in this world needs to be measured by [political correctness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_correctness "Political correctness")".[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-70)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Reception")]

Chiung Yao's romance novels were very well received in Taiwan, and by the 1990s, she was also one of the best-selling authors in China.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:21-5) She has since been enormously popular throughout the Chinese-speaking world.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) Chiung Yao's readership and viewership are predominantly female, owing to her emphasis on the feelings of young women.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-71) Her biggest sellers are _Outside the Window_ and _Deep Is the Courtyard_ (1969), which have been repeatedly reprinted.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) She is often regarded as among the most popular and foremost contemporary romance novelists in the Chinese-speaking world.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-72)

Her novels have been praised for the [prose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prose "Prose"), the poetry that is part of her earlier works, and the literary allusions of their titles.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) The Columbia Companion to Modern East Asian Literature states the novels are sometimes described as "morbid", as some feature socially or ethically questionable romantic relationships (e.g. between teacher and student).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-Mostow2003-6) Her romance novels and their film adaptions have been criticized for their [melodramatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melodrama "Melodrama")[plotlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plotline "Plotline")[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-73)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-74) and long-winded dialogues.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-75)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Personal life")]

### Family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Family")]

Chiung Yao's second husband was Ping Hsin-tao, the head of Crown Publishing, with whom she had an eight-year extramarital affair before their marriage.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-z235-55) Her father, Chen Chih-ping, was a professor in the Department of Chinese Literature at National Taiwan Normal University.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:19-14) Her mother, Yuan Hsing-shu, taught Chinese at [Taipei Municipal Chien Kuo High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei_Municipal_Chien_Kuo_High_School "Taipei Municipal Chien Kuo High School").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:19-14) Her maternal grandfather, Yuan Li-chen, served as the first president of the Bank of Communications.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:6-12) Her maternal grandmother, Tseng Yi, was self-taught and excelled in poetry and painting. She was also a nationally renowned female physician in China.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:6-12) Her granduncle, [Yuan Li-zhun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_Li-zhun?action=edit&redlink=1 "Yuan Li-zhun (page does not exist)")[[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%A2%81%E5%8B%B5%E6%BA%96 "zh:袁勵準")], was a tutor to the [Xuantong Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xuantong_Emperor "Xuantong Emperor").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:6-12) Her aunt, [Yuan Jing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_Jing_(writer) "Yuan Jing (writer)"), was a writer, and another aunt, [Yuan Xiaoyuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_Xiaoyuan "Yuan Xiaoyuan"), was China's first female diplomat and tax official.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:6-12)

### Religion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chiung_Yao&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Religion")]

Chiung Yao was an [atheist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atheism "Atheism"). In her later years, she expressed respect for religion on multiple occasions but consistently rejected any form of [proselytisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proselytism "Proselytism") or religious rituals. She regarded ghosts and deities as elements of literature and drama and rejected the possibility of their existence in reality. She advocated confronting life by enriching oneself rather than relying on religion or [superstitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superstition "Superstition").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:20-76)

In her will, she explicitly requested that no religious practices be used to commemorate her - such as setting up a mourning hall, burning [joss paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_paper "Joss paper"), or holding traditional rituals like the "seven-day rites". Instead, she expressed a preference for an [eco-friendly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eco-friendly "Eco-friendly") flower burial. She emphasized that death was a deeply personal matter and should not impose a burden on others.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiung_Yao#cite_note-:20-76)
