## Founded in 1995 by Dan Simon, and named for the seven authors who committed to a home with a fiercely independent spirit, Seven Stories Press publishes uncompromising political books, fiction, and poetry.

**A little history**

The Seven Stories story began in 1983–84, when Dan Simon came across a story by Nelson Algren called “A Bottle of Milk for Mother” in an old anthology edited by Robert Penn Warren that Simon bought from a street vendor for a dollar. He then read everything Algren wrote that he could find and discovered that Algren’s books—all of them—had been allowed to go out of print. Simon’s friend and colleague Glenn Thompson, founder and publisher of Writers and Readers Publishing, encouraged Simon to see if he could obtain the rights, offering to give him his own imprint and to cover the printing costs. The first books—_The Neon Wilderness_, then _Never Come Morning—_ were published as “Dan Simon/Four Walls Eight Windows” books at Writers and Readers, which at the time was distributed in the US by W.W. Norton, where Simon was working as an assistant editor after grad school when he met Glenn. The Algren books sold well, and got some attention.

In 1985, Simon formed a partnership with another young editor, John Oakes, who was at Grove. Together they incorporated and raised some funds in 1986. Thompson let them have the remaining stock of the early Algren reprints for good luck.

After ten years as an independent literary and political press under the co-direction of Simon and Oakes, Four Walls Eight Windows bifurcated and the two editors went their separate ways as independent book publishers, each taking their respective halves of the Four Walls list, Oakes continuing to use the Four Walls Eight Windows name, and Simon as founder in 1995 of Seven Stories Press—named in honor of the first seven authors at Four Walls Eight Windows who chose to join him on the adventure: Octavia E. Butler, Annie Ernaux, Gary Null, Project Censored, Charley Rosen, Vassilis Vassilikos, and the estate of Nelson Algren. After the first seven came another 20 or so. But without the first seven Simon said that he would not have set out for a second time as founder of a new independent press. The first book under the new imprint was Vassilikos’s _And Dreams Are Dreams…,_ a collection of three novellas that appeared in the fall of 1995 from the author of the celebrated political thriller, _Z_, the basis for the Costa-Gavras film of the same name.

**Fiercely Independent**

Seven Stories publishes works of the human imagination—sometimes in the form of fiction and literature, sometimes in the form of political nonfiction and sometimes in a hybrid form that has elements of both. Our books may be written originally in English or in other languages—as much as 25% of our list in any given season may be works in translation from the French, Spanish, Italian, Greek, Arabic, Russian, Swedish, Polish, Korean, or Vietnamese among other languages—or, as is true of many of the works of Ariel Dorfman, written in two languages simultaneously, the author going back and forth between English and Spanish until the text is complete.

Whether political or literary or both together, Seven Stories is as well known for publishing on human rights, social and economic justice, and media as for its prize-winning American fiction, literature in translation, and poetry collections. We believe that the mix here of politics and fiction, of protest and celebration, of militancy and tenderness is important. Our credo is that publishers have a special responsibility to defend free speech and human rights, and to celebrate the gifts of the human imagination wherever we can.

Whether publishing the _zeitgeist­-_ changing fiction of American masters Kate Braverman, Octavia E. Butler, Rick DeMarinis, Barry Gifford, Peter Plate and Chavisa Woods, newsbreaking investigative reporting by Greg Palast or Loretta Napoleoni, the bestselling late writings of Kurt Vonnegut (including _New York Times_ hardcover bestseller _A Man without a Country_), National Book Award-winning _Poems Seven_ by Alan Dugan, _Greed_ by Nobel Prize-winner Elfriede Jelinek, the 2016 Mildred L. Batchelder Honor Book Award-winning middle-grade novel _Adam & Thomas_ by Aharon Appelfeld, the 2016 Stonewall Book Award-winning _Sex Is a Funny Word_, or Kia Corthron’s _The Castle Cross the Magnet Carter_, currently shortlisted for the Center for Fiction First Novel Prize, Seven Stories earns its reputation for bringing books that might otherwise have been marginalized thunderously into the mainstream conversation.

Seven Stories publishes two major annual books each year, Human Rights Watch’s _World Report_, which catalogues the changing human rights situation in over 90 countries and territories; and Project Censored’s _Censored_, which tracks the news that in a highly functioning democracy would be on the front pages of every metropolitan daily and leading the evening news broadcast, but in our country is relegated to so-called alternative publications. Noam Chomsky wrote us recently in praise of Project Censored on the occasion of its 40 th anniversary this year, citing “_its remarkable achievements, both in bringing to us critically important stories that have had little or no media attention and in engaging young activists who will be able to carry on this very valuable work. A crucial contribution to the hope for a more just and democratic society._” For twenty-five of its 40 years, Project Censored has partnered with Seven Stories.

These annuals arrive each year alongside pioneering nonfiction from Russell Banks, Kate Bornstein, Noam Chomsky, Angela Davis, Jack Forbes, Shere Hite, Derrick Jensen, Kalle Lasn, Inga Muscio, Ralph Nader, Hal Niedzvicki, Loretta Napoleoni, Barbara Seaman, Howard Zinn and so many others. They are joined on the Seven Stories list by necessary works in translation from giants of the global literary and political scene like Assia Djebar, Ariel Dorfman, Marguerite Duras, Annie Ernaux, Jean Giono, Hwang Sok-yong, and Vassilis Vassilikos, and prominent and important fresh voices like Wojciech Jagielski, Lola Lafon, and Abdella Taïa. Seven Stories is also pioneering graphic works that range from Ted Rall’s bestselling political biographies, to the exquisite and bestselling Graphic Canon anthologies edited by Russ Kick that have introduced hundreds of illustrators and graphic artists to a new reading public, and re-introduced the world’s classic literature—arguably humankind’s most important and lasting legacy—to a new generation of readers discovering Shakespeare, Sappho, Dante, and so many other great writers for the first time in the form of ingenious and transformative graphics.

**A little more history**

One of our most influential books was Noam Chomsky’s _9-11_, an Open Media pamphlet edited by Greg Ruggiero which came out in November 2001, only seven weeks after the events of that day. It was published as a cry in the wilderness from a dissident voice then not widely known outside of academia at a moment when the concerted American response to the tragedy was the bombing of Afghanistan. But within two years it was not only a worldwide bestseller, selling 400,000 copies in the US and over a million across the globe, but more importantly had become the emblem of a nascent resistance movement here, one which by 2003 then-President George W. Bush was finding it necessary to deny in presidential press conferences. _9-11_ showed the world that there were other voices in America that did not agree with the policies of our government. Many other titles we have published, by writers like Barry Gifford, Angela Davis, Assia Djebar, Annie Ernaux, Kurt Vonnegut, and Howard Zinn to name just a few, have changed how large numbers see themselves and the world around them, shifting the conversation and bringing courage and true storytelling to bear. But it may well have been _9-11_, so small a book physically that we called it a pamphlet, that best shows how a book can stake out a claim that will bring about change decades or even generations later.

Weeks before the presidential election of 2012, and then again in the weeks before the 2016 presidential election, Seven Stories partnered with bestselling investigative reporter Greg Palast to publish _Billionaires & Ballot Bandits_ and _The Best Democracy Money Can Buy_, to inform Americans of voting system irregularities that were disenfranchising minority voters across the nation. In 2012 the story was broken on the front page of _The Nation_ magazine and embraced by unions in Ohio especially, who toured Palast extensively to their members. In 2016, after _Rolling Stone_ broke the story, Palast paired the book with an extraordinary documentary movie. In both cases, he was able to inform people at a key moment in our nation’s history about events that were not being reported extensively in the media and that were having a tremendous impact on our democracy.

And then there are the writers here who cross back and forth across the line between politics and literature constantly—Linh Dinh, Beverly Gologorsky, Innosanto Nagara, Peter Plate, Anne Roiphe, Cory Silverberg, Chavisa Woods, to name just a few, not to mention Lee Stringer and Kurt Vonnegut—who came from opposite ends of the American dream and became true friends at Seven Stories. Some Seven Stories authors publish their fiction and their nonfiction with us—Linh Dinh, Ariel Dorfman, Kurt Vonnegut, to name a few, while others publish both books for adults and books for young adults or children with us—including Barry Gifford, Andri Snaer Magnason, Howard Zinn, to name a few; and some in both English and Spanish—for example Noam Chomsky, Ariel Dorfman, Innosanto Nagara, and Howard Zinn.

**Our philosophy and vision**

One of the characteristics of our catalogue we are most proud of is that one-book authors are a rarity. The norm is for our authors, including many of our most successful who could publish anywhere, to choose to stay with Seven Stories, and also for us to stay with the authors on our list. It is more common to see six or eight or ten books from one author on our list than to see only one. We think this shows that once our authors know us well, they want to keep on with us; and that the better we know our authors, the better we are able to publish them well.

Under the direction of publisher Dan Simon, perhaps no other small independent house in America has consistently attracted so many important voices away from corporate publishing. Part of our goal is to at least provide a viable alternative, so that writers who would rather go with a smaller, independent, politically engaged publisher, where profits from bestsellers are redirected towards the acquisition of books that might not otherwise be published, and where there is a guiding social mission, at least have the choice. Authors of note should not have to feel that the only publishers are the corporate ones. Seven Stories isn’t the only such publisher, needless to say. We’re part of a vibrant community of smaller houses doing great work, like Akashic, Beacon, Bellevue Literary, Cinco Puntos, Coach House, Coffeehouse, Ig, Feminist, Graywolf, Haymarket, Melville House, Monthly Review, Milkweed, New Press, OR Books, Other Press, Parallax, and Verso, to name just a handful of the presses in this vibrant counter-culture, each one with its own strengths.

On several notable occasions, Seven Stories has stepped in to publish important books that were being refused the right to publish for political reasons, including _Dark Alliance: The CIA, the Contras and the Crack Cocaine Explosion_ by Pulitzer Prize–winning journalist Gary Webb, _Citizen Newhouse_ by Carol Felsenthal, _The Others_ by pseudonymous Saudi Arabian queer author Seba al-Herz, _All Things Censored_ by distinguished journalist and activist Mumia Abu-Jamal, _My Times: A Memoir of Dissent_ by John L. Hess, and _10,000 Dresses_ by Marcus Ewert and Rex Ray. But much of what we do in defense of free speech is more nuanced. We keep all our books in print. The only time we will put an edition of a book out of print is when we have another edition of the same book in print that is either more affordable or more up to date. For example, we will let a hardcover go out of print once there is a paperback out that replaces it. And we will do a less commercial, or even a less narrative work by an author whose more commercial books we also publish.

Seven Stories is the authors we publish and the books they write. Seven Stories is also the people who work here and contribute on a daily basis to the books and to the ongoing project, or have worked here and take something of their experience here with them when and wherever they go. In our catalogue we name our current staff, our foreign agents and distributors, and our board of advisors, but also, as “fellow travelers,” key former staff that continue to bring us projects or help our work in other ways. Were you not to read a single book, but came and visited and met the people who work at Seven Stories, you might come away with the same complete sense of Seven Stories and the books we publish. Funny thing.

We are completely independent. We publish in English, in Spanish, in hardcover, and paperback, usually with simultaneous e-book editions in all major e-formats, books as long as 1,500 pages, and pamphlets or children’s books as short as 28 pages, for adults, for young adults and for children. Occasionally we have produced our own audiobooks (though far more often we sublicense the audio rights to our books to audiobook publishers).

**Editorial Siete Cuentos**

Launched in 2000, Seven Stories’ Spanish-language imprint, Editorial Siete Cuentos, represents a major ongoing effort on the part of Seven Stories to introduce important English-language texts to Spanish-language readers. Siete Cuentos has published Spanish-language editions of _Our Bodies, Ourselves_ (_Nuestros cuerpos, nuestras vidas_) and Howard Zinn’s _A People’s History of the United States_ (_La otra historia de los Estados Unidos_.) Siete Cuentos has published new and classic works of literature by Ariel Dorfman, including _Death and the Maiden_ (_La muerte y la doncella_) and _Heading South, Looking North_ (_Rumbo al sur, deseando el norte_), as well as fiction by Ángela Vallvey and Sonia Rivera-Valdés. We selectively publish new works in separate English and Spanish editions, as for example with Julia Alvarez’s _Where Do They Go_, an illustrated children’s book from a poem about the experience of loss.

**Triangle Square Books for Young Readers**

We see children and young adults as active readers and doers who will change the world for the better. Triangle Square Books for Young Readers breathes progressive new life into the world of children's and YA books through our inclusive imprint, which features such titles as the award-winning _10,000 Dresses_ by Marcus Ewert and Rex Ray, Innosanto Nagara's _A is for Activist_, the runaway hit board book for the children of the ninety-nine percent (in both Spanish and English), Cory Silverberg's _What Makes a Baby?_ and _Sex Is A Funny Word_, and our _For Young People_ series, which adapts celebrated nonfiction books for middle grade readers and to date includes seminal works by Howard Zinn on a people's history of the US, Charles C. Mann on globalism, Jared Diamond on evolutionary biology, and Ronald Takaki on the history of multiculturalism. Triangle Square books are published in hardcover, paperback, and e-book formats, in English and Spanish, throughout North America and around the world. Triangle Square supports social justice, multicultural literacy, restoration of the environment, kids’ rights, and freedom of the imagination.

**Seven Stories Press UK**

In 2016, we opened Seven Stories Press UK, a British company, to bring out Seven Stories and Triangle Square titles in England in a homegrown way, initially featuring a modest and highly selective list, and with the hope of some day also being able to originate titles from England for the U.S. and the rest of the English speaking world.

Together with Seven Stories Press in New York, the new UK arm stands for uncompromising works of fiction, politics and non-fiction, written by both established and emerging authors with a range of minority and diverse voices. We also publish books for progressive children, baby radicals and curious kids of all stripes. Seven Stories Press UK will be bringing UK readers the same level of imaginative writing, radical ideas—and good parties—that have marked Seven Stories Press in the US for more than twenty years. So far, our February 2017 launch event for SSP UK, featuring readings from Kia Corthron’s _The Castle Cross the Magnet Carter_, was standing-room only with a boisterous crowd of local literati and industry insiders.

**Parting Thoughts**

At Seven Stories we see books as tokens of friendship, and often enough friendship also arises from the work we do on these books and the close association that work often requires. Some years ago the historian and Seven Stories author Howard Zinn called and asked us to introduce him to a writer he much admired, fellow Seven Storian Kurt Vonnegut. We did, and it turned out that Kurt was already an avid reader of Howard’s books. The two became fast friends for the rest of their lives. As we’ve been taught by many of the authors we work with—Jared Diamond, Derrick Jensen, Howard Zinn, Noam Chomsky, Peter Plate, Octavia Butler and Barry Gifford to name just a few—the human species is fickle and is often dangerous to itself and to others. Friendship, though, seems to be, if not an answer to that problem then at least a tempering quality that isn’t unique to humans necessarily, but let’s say is a tender and tempering quality we share with other animals that can help us bring positive change to all aspects of the things we do.

Regarding bookselling culture, Seven Stories publishes Andy Laties’s _Rebel Bookseller_, and Loren Glass’s _Rebel Publisher:Grove Press and the Revolution of the Word_, and has other related projects in the works. We believe the independent bookseller community in America to be an historically significant one and we engage with local independent booksellers as much as possible.

Our friends at Penguin Random House provide us with the world’s most efficient and effective sales and distribution. And not enough can be said about American librarians—said, and then said again, and again. Without the librarians and booksellers, we couldn’t do what we do. About the former, Kurt Vonnegut famously wrote, “The America I loved still exists, if not in the White House, the Supreme Court, the Senate, the House of Representatives, or the media. The America I loved still exists at the front desks of our public libraries.”

Finally, we wish to express here our thanks and appreciation to the members of our advisory board (Russell Banks, Athol Fugard, Juris Jurjevics, Raoul Peck, Peter Sellars, Claire Tisne, Minky Worden, and the late, great Dore Ashton), to our staff, to our authors, and to our readers, since without you all no statement of who we are would be complete.

**Simon & Schuster LLC** ([/ˈ ʃ uː s t ər/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_SHOO-stər_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")) is an American publishing house owned by [Kohlberg Kravis Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kohlberg_Kravis_Roberts "Kohlberg Kravis Roberts") since 2023. It was founded in New York City in 1924, by [Richard L. Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_L._Simon "Richard L. Simon") and [M. Lincoln Schuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._Lincoln_Schuster "M. Lincoln Schuster").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-5) Along with [Penguin Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin_Random_House "Penguin Random House"), [Hachette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hachette_Book_Group_USA "Hachette Book Group USA"), [HarperCollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HarperCollins "HarperCollins") and [Macmillan Publishers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macmillan_Publishers "Macmillan Publishers"), Simon & Schuster is considered one of the ["Big Five"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Five_(publishers) "Big Five (publishers)") English-language publishers. As of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simon_%26_Schuster&action=edit), Simon & Schuster was the third largest publisher in the United States,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-6) publishing 2,000 titles annually under 35 different [imprints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imprint_(trade_name) "Imprint (trade name)").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:4-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-8)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simon_%26_Schuster&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Early years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simon_%26_Schuster&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early years")]

In 1924, [Richard Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_L._Simon "Richard L. Simon")'s aunt, a [crossword puzzle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossword_puzzle "Crossword puzzle") enthusiast, asked whether there was a book of _[New York World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_World "New York World")_ crossword puzzles, which were popular at the time. After discovering that none had been published, Simon and [Max Schuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._Lincoln_Schuster "M. Lincoln Schuster") decided to launch a company to exploit the opportunity.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-allen-9) At the time, Simon was a piano salesman and Schuster was editor of an automotive trade magazine.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:3-10) They pooled US$8,000, equivalent to $150,000 today[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-inflation-US-11) and started a company that published crossword puzzles.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-Another-12)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-allen-9)

The new publishing house used "fad" publishing to publish books that exploited current fads and trends. Simon called this "planned publishing".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:3-10) Instead of signing authors with a planned manuscript, they came up with their own ideas, and then hired writers to carry them out.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:3-10)

In the 1930s, the publisher moved to "Publisher's Row" on [Park Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Avenue "Park Avenue") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"), New York.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:3-10)

### Expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simon_%26_Schuster&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Expansion")]

In 1939, Simon & Schuster backed Robert Fair de Graff to found [Pocket Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pocket_Books "Pocket Books"), America's first paperback publisher.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-13) In 1942, Simon & Schuster and [Western Publishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Publishing "Western Publishing") launched the [Little Golden Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Golden_Books "Little Golden Books") series in cooperation with the Artists and Writers Guild.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-15)

In 1944, [Marshall Field III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Field_III "Marshall Field III"), owner of the _[Chicago Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago\_Sun "Chicago Sun")_, purchased Simon & Schuster and Pocket Books.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-16) The company was sold back to Simon & Schuster following his death in 1957 [[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-17) for $1 million.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-18)

In the 1950s and 1960s, many publishers including Simon & Schuster turned toward educational publishing due to the [baby boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby_boom "Baby boom") market.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:8-19) Pocket Books focused on paperbacks for the educational market instead of textbooks and started the Washington Square Press imprint in 1959.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:8-19) By 1964, it had published more than 200 titles and was expected to put out another 400 by the end of that year.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:8-19) Books published under the imprint included classic reprints such as _[Lorna Doone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorna\_Doone "Lorna Doone")_, _[Ivanhoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivanhoe "Ivanhoe")_, _[Tom Sawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom\_Sawyer "Tom Sawyer")_, _[Huckleberry Finn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huckleberry\_Finn "Huckleberry Finn")_, and _[Robinson Crusoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robinson\_Crusoe "Robinson Crusoe")_.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-20) In 1967, Simon & Schuster acquired Monarch Press Publishing, Inc. with its extensive line of college and high school study guides.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-21)

In 1960, Richard Simon died of a heart attack; six years later, Max Schuster retired and sold his half of Simon & Schuster to Leon Shimkin.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-Another-12)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:2-22) Shimkin then merged Simon & Schuster with Pocket Books under the name of Simon & Schuster.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-Another-12)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:2-22) In 1968, editor-in-chief [Robert Gottlieb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Gottlieb "Robert Gottlieb"), who had worked at Simon & Schuster since 1955 and edited several bestsellers including [Joseph Heller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Heller "Joseph Heller")'s _[Catch-22](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catch-22 "Catch-22")_,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-23) left abruptly to work at competitor [Knopf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_A._Knopf "Alfred A. Knopf"), taking along influential S&S employees [Nina Bourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nina_Bourne "Nina Bourne") and Tony Schulte.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-24)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-Another-12)

On January 28, 1975, Simon & Schuster was acquired by [Gulf+Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_and_Western_Industries "Gulf and Western Industries") in an 8-for-1 [stock swap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_swap "Stock swap").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-25) Four years later, in 1979, Richard Snyder was named CEO. Over the next several years he would help the company to grow substantially.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-auto-26)

### 1980s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simon_%26_Schuster&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1980s")]

After the death of Gulf+Western head [Charles Bluhdorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Bluhdorn "Charles Bluhdorn") on February 19, 1983,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-27) the publishing company made the decision to diversify. Bluhdorn's successor Martin Davis told _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_, "Society was undergoing dramatic changes so that there was a greater need for textbooks, maps, and educational information. We saw the opportunity to diversify into those areas, which are more stable and more profitable than trade publishing."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:1-28)

In 1984, Simon & Schuster under CEO [Richard E. Snyder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_E._Snyder "Richard E. Snyder") acquired educational publisher Esquire Corporation, owner of companies including [Allyn & Bacon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allyn_&_Bacon "Allyn & Bacon") (and former owner of _[Esquire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esquire\_(magazine) "Esquire (magazine)")_ magazine), for $180 million.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:1-28)[Prentice Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prentice_Hall "Prentice Hall") was brought into the company fold in 1985 for $700 million, viewed by some executives as a catalyst to change the company as a whole.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-Another-12)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:1-28) This acquisition was followed by [Silver Burdett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_Burdett "Silver Burdett") in 1986,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:0-29) mapmaker [Gousha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gousha "Gousha") in 1987 and Charles E. Simon in 1988.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:0-29) Part of the acquisition included educational publisher Allyn & Bacon which, according to then editor and chief [Michael Korda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Korda "Michael Korda"), became the "nucleus of S&S's educational and informational business".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-Another-12) Three California educational companies were also purchased between 1988 and 1990–Quercus, Fearon Education and Janus Book Publishers.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:1-28) In all, Simon & Schuster spent more than $1 billion in acquisitions between 1983 and 1991.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:0-29)

In the 1980s, Snyder also made an unsuccessful bid toward video publishing, At the start, Snyder was dismayed to realize that though Simon & Schuster had a huge bestseller in _Jane Fonda's Workout Book_, they did not own the rights to the VHS, which was earning even better. This prompted Snyder to ask editors to obtain video rights for every new book. Agents were often reluctant to give these up, and the S&S Video division never took off. However, in 1985 Simon & Schuster then launched its profitable audiobook division,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-30) which became a major business for the company by the 1990s.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-Another-12)

In 1989, Gulf and Western Inc., owner of Simon & Schuster, changed its name to [Paramount Communications Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Communications "Paramount Communications")[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-31)

### 1990s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simon_%26_Schuster&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1990s")]

In 1990, _The New York Times_ described Simon & Schuster as the largest book publisher in the United States, with sales of $1.3 billion the previous year.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:1-28) That same year, Simon & Schuster acquired the children's publisher Green Tiger Press.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-32)

In 1993, Simon & Schuster bought [Macmillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macmillan_Inc. "Macmillan Inc.") (including [Scribner's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Scribner's_Sons "Charles Scribner's Sons"), [Free Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Press_(publisher) "Free Press (publisher)"), and Jossey-Bass), and changed its name to Paramount Publishing. [Viacom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viacom_(1971%E2%80%932006) "Viacom (1971–2006)") then bought Paramount in 1994 and changed the name back to Simon & Schuster.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-34) Macmillan was acquired for US$552.8 million.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-35) Later that year, Snyder was suddenly fired from S&S and was replaced by the company's president and chief operating officer Jonathan Newcomb.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-auto-26) Simon & Schuster then sold several peripheral assets, such as selling Charles E. Simon Co. to CDB Infotek.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-36) Gousha was sold to [Rand McNally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rand_McNally "Rand McNally") in 1996.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-37)

In 1994, S&S acquired the software operations of [Markt+Technik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markt+Technik "Markt+Technik").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-38) Later that year, Simon & Schuster (through Paramount) launched a software publisher in partnership with [Davidson & Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davidson_&_Associates "Davidson & Associates") named Simon & Schuster Interactive.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-39) The studio published video games such as _[Outlaw Golf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outlaw\_Golf "Outlaw Golf")_, _[Deer Avenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deer\_Avenger "Deer Avenger")_, _[I.M. Meen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I.M.\_Meen "I.M. Meen")_, _[Chill Manor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chill\_Manor "Chill Manor")_, _[EVE Online](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EVE\_Online "EVE Online")_, and games based on [Richard Scarry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Scarry "Richard Scarry")'s characters. S&S Interactive shut down in 2003.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-40)

In 1998, Viacom sold Simon & Schuster's educational operations (including Prentice Hall, Macmillan, and Jossey-Bass) to [Pearson plc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson_plc "Pearson plc"), the global publisher and then owner of Penguin and the _[Financial Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial\_Times "Financial Times")_; Pearson then merged the operations with [Addison-Wesley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addison-Wesley "Addison-Wesley")[Longman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longman "Longman") to form [Pearson Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearson_Education "Pearson Education"). Later, Pearson sold several of the acquired S&S divisions: first Appleton & Lange was divested to [McGraw-Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McGraw-Hill_Education "McGraw-Hill Education") and Master Data Central was sold to [Master Data Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_Data_Center "Master Data Center").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-41) Then, Jossey-Bass was sold to [John Wiley & Sons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wiley_&_Sons "John Wiley & Sons") and the Bureau of Business Practice was sold to [Wolters Kluwer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolters_Kluwer "Wolters Kluwer").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-42) Subsequently, Macmillan Library Reference's children's imprints (Silver Burdett Press, Dillon Press, Crestwood House, Silver Press, New Discovery and [Julian Messner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Messner "Julian Messner")) were closed.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-43) Then, [Gale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gale_(publisher) "Gale (publisher)") acquired Macmillan Library Reference (Charles Scribner's Sons Reference, Macmillan Reference, Thorndike Press, [G.K. Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G._K._Hall_&_Co. "G. K. Hall & Co."), Twayne Publishers and Schirmer Books).[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-44) Finally, [IDG Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IDG_Books "IDG Books") acquired Macmillan General Reference (including [Frommer's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frommer's "Frommer's"), [J.K. Lasser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_K._Lasser "Jacob K. Lasser"), [Betty Crocker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Crocker "Betty Crocker") Cookbooks, [Weight Watchers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WW_International "WW International") Dieting and Cookbooks and Howell House Pet Books but excluding [Complete Idiot's Guides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complete_Idiot's_Guides "Complete Idiot's Guides"), which Pearson later transferred to Macmillan Computer Publishing under [Alpha Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Books "Alpha Books") and currently part of [Penguin Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin_Random_House "Penguin Random House") under [Dorling Kindersley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DK_(publisher) "DK (publisher)")).[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-46)

### 2000s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simon_%26_Schuster&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2000s")]

In 2002, Simon & Schuster acquired its Canadian distributor Distican.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-47) Simon & Schuster began publishing in Canada in 2013.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-48)

At the end of 2005, Viacom split into two companies: [CBS Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Corporation "CBS Corporation") (which inherited S&S and [Paramount Parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Parks "Paramount Parks")), and the other retaining the [Viacom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viacom_(2005%E2%80%932019) "Viacom (2005–2019)") name.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-49) Also in 2005, Simon & Schuster acquired Strebor Books International, which was founded in 1999 by author Kristina Laferne Roberts, who has written under the pseudonym "Zane".[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-bloomberg.com-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-51) A year later, in 2006, Simon & Schuster launched the conservative imprint [Threshold Editions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threshold_Editions "Threshold Editions").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-52)

In 2009, Simon & Schuster signed a multi-book and co-publishing deal with [Glenn Beck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Beck "Glenn Beck") which appeared under many of its imprints and included adult non-fiction, fiction, children, and YA literature as well as e-book and audiobook originals.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-53) As part of CBS, Simon & Schuster has been the primary publisher for books related to various media franchises owned by and/or aired on CBS such as [CSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSI:_Crime_Scene_Investigation "CSI: Crime Scene Investigation").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-54) The company has also held a license to publish books in the _[Star Trek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star\_Trek "Star Trek")_ franchise under [Pocket Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pocket_Books "Pocket Books").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-55)

### 2010s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simon_%26_Schuster&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2010s")]

In 2011, Simon & Schuster signed a number of co-publishing deals. Glenn Beck signed a new co-publishing deal with Simon & Schuster for his own imprint, [Mercury Ink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TheBlaze "TheBlaze").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-56) Under Atria, Simon & Schuster also launched a publishing venture with [Cash Money Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cash_Money_Records "Cash Money Records") called Cash Money Content.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-57)

On April 11, 2012, the United States Department of Justice filed _[United States v. Apple Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United\_States\_v.\_Apple\_(2012) "United States v. Apple (2012)")_, naming [Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc."), Simon & Schuster, and four other major publishers as defendants. The suit alleged that they conspired to fix prices for [e-books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-books "E-books"), and weaken [Amazon.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon.com "Amazon.com")'s position in the market, in violation of [antitrust law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_antitrust_law "United States antitrust law").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-washington_post_DOJ_sues-58)

Simon & Schuster reorganized all of their imprints under four main groups in 2012.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:9-59) The four groups included the Atria Publishing Group, the Scribner Publishing Group, the Simon & Schuster Publishing Group and the Gallery Publishing Group.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:9-59) According to CEO [Carolyn Reidy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolyn_Reidy "Carolyn Reidy"), the divisions were created to align imprints that complement one another and that the structure would "lead to a sharper editorial focus for our imprints even as it takes consideration of the natural affinities among them."[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:9-59) In 2012, Simon & Schuster launched a self-publishing arm of the company, Archway Publishing.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-60)

On November 14, 2013, Simon & Schuster signed a co-publishing agreement with former [New York Yankees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Yankees "New York Yankees") shortstop, [Derek Jeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Jeter "Derek Jeter"), to launch Jeter Publishing.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-61) In December 2013, a federal judge approved a settlement of the antitrust claims, in which Simon & Schuster and the other publishers paid into a fund that provided credits to customers who had overpaid for books due to the price-fixing.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-usatoday_settlements_rolling_out-62)

In 2014, Simon & Schuster signed a partnership deal with Amazon over ebooks and also launched a new speculative fiction imprint. On October 21, 2014, Simon & Schuster signed a multi-year partnership deal with [Amazon.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon.com "Amazon.com") in negotiations concerning the price of e-books.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-63) Simon & Schuster also launched a new science fiction imprint called Simon451 that would publish titles across science fiction and fantasy with an emphasis on ebooks and online communities.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:11-64) The name of the imprint was inspired by [Ray Bradbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Bradbury "Ray Bradbury")'s book _[Fahrenheit 451](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fahrenheit\_451 "Fahrenheit 451")_ (the temperature at which books burn).[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:11-64) Bradbury's classic is also published by Simon & Schuster.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:11-64)

Simon & Schuster expanded beyond book publishing in 2015 by offering a new business model and additional services for authors. In 2015, Simon & Schuster announced the creation of a new publishing unit and imprint called North Star Way.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:10-65) The imprint would publish non-fiction titles such as self-improvement, inspirational and mind-body-spirit titles. In addition, the group would also serve as a platform and set of services for authors that go beyond what a traditional book publisher offers to find their audience.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:10-65) The services include helping authors expand their reach through online courses, seminars, workshops, mobile applications, video and audiobooks, sponsorships and business partnerships, and podcasts. North Star Way sits within the [Gallery Publishing Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallery_Publishing_Group "Gallery Publishing Group") division.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:10-65) According to Michele Martin, publisher and founder, the name North Star reflects their mission, "to publish books that will help readers find the path to a better life, and to be a guide for our authors, not only through publication of their books but also in the many other activities that can help their message find the widest possible audience."[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-66) In an interview with _[Kirkus Reviews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirkus\_Reviews "Kirkus Reviews")_, Michele Martin expanded that North Star Way, "aims to meet consumers where they are, in whatever form of media they consume. We expand the ideas in the books into a variety of platforms."[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-67) The name prompted [Marvel Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Comics "Marvel Comics") to attempt to register the name of their superhero [Northstar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northstar_(character) "Northstar (character)") in February 2015. The application was denied as Simon & Schuster had already made a trademark application for North Star Way in January.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-68)

Simon & Schuster launched SimonSays.com a portal for online video courses in 2016, along with Scout Press, a new literary fiction imprint under Gallery Books Group. They also launched North Star Way, a platform-based program to provide authors with services beyond publishing including brand management, online courses, sponsorship, and business partnerships.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:4-7) Also as of 2016, Simon & Schuster had more than 18k e-books available for sale and signed a deal to distribute Start Publishing LLC, a catalog of 7,000 e-book titles.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:4-7)

In 2019, CBS and Viacom reunited to form ViacomCBS. As a result, Simon & Schuster became part of the newly formed ViacomCBS.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-69) Since February 15, 2022, ViacomCBS is known as [Paramount Global](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Global "Paramount Global").

### 2020s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simon_%26_Schuster&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2020s")]

In March 2020, ViacomCBS CEO [Bob Bakish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bakish "Robert Bakish") announced the company's intention to sell the Simon & Schuster division, as it "does not have significant connection for our broader business."[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-70) Bakish expected the sale to close in 2020, a date that was delayed by the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-71)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-72)

In May 2020, the company's CEO [Carolyn Reidy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolyn_Reidy "Carolyn Reidy") died unexpectedly from a [heart attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_attack "Heart attack").[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-73) Jonathan Karp was appointed as her replacement.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:5-74)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:6-75)

A purchase by German media group [Bertelsmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertelsmann "Bertelsmann") was eventually blocked on anti-trust grounds. In September 2020 [Bertelsmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bertelsmann "Bertelsmann"), which owns [Penguin Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin_Random_House "Penguin Random House"), announced that it was interested in acquiring Simon & Schuster. According to Bertelsmann chief executive and chairman [Thomas Rabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Rabe_(manager) "Thomas Rabe (manager)"), "We've been the most active player on the consolidation of the book publishing market in the last 10 years. We combined [Penguin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin_Group "Penguin Group") and [Random House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_House "Random House") very successfully to create by far the largest book publisher in the world, actually the only global book publisher. Given this position we would, of course, be interested in Simon & Schuster."[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-76)[Vivendi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivendi "Vivendi"), which owns the French publisher [Editis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Editis "Editis"), and [News Corp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_Corp "News Corp"), which owns [HarperCollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HarperCollins "HarperCollins"), were also named as contenders in acquiring Simon & Schuster. [ViacomCBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_Global "Paramount Global") expected the bids to be placed before November 26, 2020.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-77) On November 25, 2020, ViacomCBS announced it would sell Simon & Schuster to Penguin Random House for $2.175 billion, with the deal expected to close in 2022.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-79)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-80) On November 2, 2021, the [United States Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice") filed a civil antitrust lawsuit to block the acquisition, arguing the combined publisher would have too much influence over books and author payments.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-81) A federal judge sided with the government, leading Paramount to nullify the deal in November 2022.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-82)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-83) An appeal to the court ruling was announced a day later by Bertelsmann,[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-84) but canceled November 21.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-85)

In 2021, Simon & Schuster made book deals with former Trump administration officials such as [Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States")[Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence") and Trump adviser [Kellyanne Conway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kellyanne_Conway "Kellyanne Conway"). This prompted protests among Simon & Schuster staff.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-86)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-88)

In 2022, Simon & Schuster employee Filippo Bernardini was arrested for the [2016–2021 literary phishing thefts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016%E2%80%932021_literary_phishing_thefts "2016–2021 literary phishing thefts"). The company released a statement saying they were "shocked and horrified to learn today of the allegations of fraud and [identity theft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_theft "Identity theft") by an employee."[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-peiserWAPO6jan2022-89)

In June 2023, _The Wall Street Journal_ reported that HarperCollins and investment firm [Kohlberg Kravis Roberts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kohlberg_Kravis_Roberts "Kohlberg Kravis Roberts") (KKR) had emerged as potential frontrunners to acquire the company.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-90) On August 3, 2023, it was reported that KKR was in "advanced talks" with Paramount Global.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-91)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-92) On August 7, 2023, Paramount Global announced that it had agreed to sell Simon & Schuster to KKR for $1.62 billion.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-93) The sale was completed on October 30, 2023.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-94)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-95)

In May 2024, Simon & Schuster acquired [Veen Bosch & Keuning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veen_Bosch_&_Keuning "Veen Bosch & Keuning") (VBK), the largest Dutch book publishing company. The acquisition includes all of VBK's imprints in the Netherlands and Belgium, as well as its sister companies, the audiobook producer [Thinium](https://www.thinium.nl/), and [Bookchoice](https://web.archive.org/web/20240517064747/https://pluimen.nl/boeken-lidmaatschap-van-bookchoice?language=en), a subscription-based platform for e-books and audiobooks. This is the first expansion of Simon & Schuster into a non-English market.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-96) In September 2024, it was announced that Simon & Schuster Australia had entered an agreement to acquire publisher [Affirm Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affirm_Press "Affirm Press").[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:5-74)

In August 2025, the company announced its CEO Jonathan Karp was stepping down from the company to launch Simon Six, a new, sister company of Simon & Schuster.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:6-75) In March 2026, Simon & Schuster announced the appointment of [Greg Greeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Greeley "Greg Greeley") as its new chief executive.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:7-97) Greeley is the first CEO appointed from outside the company.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_&_Schuster#cite_note-:7-97)
